Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- The patient is resectable.  
- Rationale:  
  • Two liver metastases (2.2 cm in segment II and 3 cm in segment V) are limited in number and size, allowing an R0 resection with preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments.  
  • Expected future liver remnant after left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) plus a segment V resection would exceed the 30 % functional liver volume threshold for a normal liver.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on staging CT.  
  • Primary left‑colon tumor is symptomatic and amenable to curative resection (left hemicolectomy).  
  • Patient has no reported comorbidities that would preclude major abdominal surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to confirm lesion number, size, and relationship to vascular structures.  
   - Perform colonoscopy with biopsy to stage the primary (T/N status) and assess for obstruction.  
   - Calculate volumetric FLR; portal vein embolization is not anticipated.  
   - Optimize nutrition, assess cardiopulmonary fitness (ASA, ECOG).  

B. Surgical phase (simultaneous resection)  
   - Perform an oncologic left hemicolectomy with primary tumor removal and adequate lymphadenectomy.  
   - Conduct liver resection: left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III) plus anatomical segment V resection (or wedge) to achieve R0 margins (>1 mm).  
   - Rationale: the liver component is minor; simultaneous surgery avoids a second laparotomy, shortens overall treatment time, and is safe when the colorectal resection is not extensive.  

C. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy within 6–8 weeks (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody given RAS‑wild‑type status).  
   - Rationale: synchronous disease, elevated pre‑operative CEA, and high‑risk primary tumor warrant systemic treatment to eradicate micrometastatic disease and improve disease‑free survival.  

D. Surveillance  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance (Minagawa et al.)

Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:

The patient is resectable.  The classification is based on the following criteria:  
- Solitary liver lesion, 2.5 cm, peripheral (segment VI) – meets technical criteria for complete R0 resection with preservation of ≥2 contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
- No additional intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease on FDG‑PET; therefore disease burden is limited to one hepatic site.  
- Future liver remnant will remain well above the 30 % functional threshold after a segmental resection of segment VI; portal vein embolization is unnecessary.  
- No reported contraindicating comorbidities or impaired liver function.  
- Although the metastasis is synchronous, the small size and solitary nature outweigh the negative predictive impact of synchrony and KRAS mutation.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative work‑up (within 2 weeks)  
   • High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to confirm lesion size, location and exclude occult disease.  
   • Full laboratory panel (LFTs, bilirubin, INR, albumin, renal function) and assessment of performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
   • Multidisciplinary confirmation of fitness for combined surgery.  
   Rationale: ensures accurate anatomic mapping and verifies that the patient can tolerate a simultaneous procedure.  

B. Short‑course neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 cycles, 6–8 weeks)  
   • Regimen: FOLFOX (or CAPEOX) ± bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF), given KRAS‑mutated status precludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   Rationale: in synchronous disease with elevated CEA (35 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation, a brief chemotherapy window tests tumor biology, may further downsize the metastasis, and provides early systemic control.  

C. Simultaneous curative‑intent surgery (within 4–6 weeks after chemotherapy)  
   • Right hemicolectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (D3) for the ileocecal primary.  
   • Anatomical segment VI resection (segmentectomy or wedge) aiming for ≥1 cm macroscopic margin (R0).  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to reconfirm absence of additional lesions.  
   Rationale: the hepatic lesion is peripheral and small, allowing a limited liver resection that can be safely combined with the colorectal operation, reducing total hospital stay and avoiding two separate recovery periods.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy and surveillance  
   • Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (additional 3–4 cycles post‑op).  
   • Follow‑up: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   Rationale: consolidates systemic disease control, addresses micrometastatic risk, and enables early detection of recurrence.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable  
- Rationale:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 1.8 cm, located in segment III – amenable to wedge resection or limited segmentectomy with preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a normal liver).  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT/MRI not reported but presumed negative by MDT).  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T3N1, limited parietal invasion, technically resectable by low anterior resection (LAR).  
  • RAS wild‑type, CEA moderately elevated but not prohibitive.  
  • Patient’s age (68) and smoking history do not preclude surgery provided functional status is acceptable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Short‑course pre‑operative radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the rectum.  
   – Rationale: Provides local control of the T3 rectal lesion, creates a treatment window for hepatic surgery, and is standard for upper rectal cancers when long‑course chemoradiation is not required.  

B. Peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (4–6 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody, e.g., cetuximab, given RAS wild‑type).  
   – Rationale: Treats micrometastatic disease, serves as a biological test of tumor aggressiveness, and may further down‑size the liver lesion if needed.  

C. Restaging imaging (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI or multiphase CT, plus chest CT) after chemotherapy.  
   – Rationale: Confirms that the hepatic metastasis remains resectable, excludes new extra‑hepatic sites, and assesses FLR volume.  

D. Coordinated surgical resection – preferred simultaneous minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic LAR + laparoscopic segment III wedge resection) performed 4–6 weeks after radiotherapy, provided the patient’s operative risk is low.  
   – Rationale: Both procedures are limited in extent; simultaneous resection avoids a second hospitalization, shortens overall treatment time, and is supported by literature for minor hepatectomy combined with low anterior resection when the primary is asymptomatic after radiotherapy.  

   If intra‑operative assessment reveals inadequate FLR or unexpected disease, convert to a staged approach (liver‑first then rectal resection 4–6 weeks later).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
(Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable).  
- Rationale:  
  • Technical factors – three metastases 2‑3 cm in segments IV, V, VI with only partial contact to the right portal branch and no radiologic invasion; these lesions can be removed with non‑anatomic or segmental resections while preserving ≥30 % future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Oncologic factors – synchronous disease, KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA (410 ng/mL) are adverse prognostic indicators; guidelines therefore favor neoadjuvant systemic therapy to test tumor biology before definitive surgery.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but confirmation is required.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging and fitness assessment  
   - Perform chest CT or PET‑CT to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Obtain full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance (or similar) and calculate FLR using volumetric CT/MRI.  
   - Record performance status (ECOG/ASA), comorbidities, and baseline labs (CBC, renal, coagulation).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate 3–4 months of a doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab), given KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents ineffective).  
   - Goal: tumor down‑staging, assess biological aggressiveness, and potentially increase R0 resection rates.  

C. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or triphasic CT) and chest imaging.  
   - Re‑evaluate FLR; if FLR remains adequate and all lesions are still resectable with clear margins, proceed to surgery.  
   - If disease progresses (new lesions, vascular invasion, or inadequate FLR), consider alternative curative options (portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy, or ablative therapies) or shift to palliative intent.  

D. Surgical phase (assuming continued resectability)  
   - Sequence: Prefer a “liver‑first” or simultaneous approach depending on patient fitness and primary‑tumor symptoms.  
   - Perform non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmentectomies of segments IV, V, VI aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm). Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and ≥30 % FLR (≥40 % if prior chemotherapy).  
   - Address the transverse colon primary with oncologic resection (right hemicolectomy) ensuring adequate lymphadenectomy; order of operations can be liver first then colon, or simultaneous if operative risk acceptable.  

E. Adjuvant therapy and surveillance  
   - Complete 6 months of postoperative systemic chemotherapy (same regimen as neoadjuvant, without bevacizumab if wound healing concerns).  
   - Follow‑up with CEA measurement and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is resectable.  Rationale: four peripheral metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) each ≤3 cm, no vascular invasion, no extra‑hepatic disease, and the distribution allows segmental or non‑anatomic resections that will preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  Assuming a normal liver, the anticipated future liver remnant (FLR) will exceed the minimum 30 % (or >40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present).  Therefore both oncologic (potential for R0 resection) and technical criteria for resectability are satisfied.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative systemic therapy (6 cycles FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody) – to assess tumor biology, lower the high CEA level, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
B. Restaging imaging (contrast‑enhanced CT or liver‑specific MRI with volumetry) after chemotherapy – to confirm disease stability, verify that all lesions remain resectable and to calculate FLR.  
C. Curative‑intent surgery – simultaneous sigmoid colectomy (segmental resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) and liver resection (segmental resections of SII/SIII and SV/VIII or combined limited anatomical resection) aiming for R0 margins while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments and adequate vascular/biliary flow.  
D. Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of 6 months total systemic therapy) – to eradicate residual microscopic disease and address the elevated pre‑operative CEA.  
If volumetric analysis after step B shows FLR <30 % (or <40 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury), modify step C to a two‑stage hepatectomy or portal vein embolization before definitive liver resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is potentially resectable.  
- Oncologic factors: only two liver metastases (size 3 cm and 4 cm), both in segments II and IVa, no reported bilobar disease, and the middle hepatic vein is preserved, satisfying the current oncologic definition that all known disease can be removed with an R0 margin while preserving vascular inflow/outflow.  
- Technical factors: Resection of segments II and IVa (or non‑anatomic wedge resections) would leave at least two contiguous segments (III + IVb + V‑VIII) with adequate inflow/outflow and an expected future liver remnant > 30 % of total liver volume, meeting the technical criteria for hepatic resection.  
- However, the primary tumor is T4N2, indicating a high‑risk primary that must be controlled first; therefore the case is classified as “potentially resectable” pending confirmation of adequate FLR and patient fitness.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Control of the primary tumor (surgical) – Perform a right hemicolectomy (or extended right hemicolectomy if required for T4 involvement) as the first operative step. Rationale: the primary is locally advanced (T4) and symptomatic control (obstruction, bleeding) is prioritized; resection also provides pathological staging and reduces tumor‑related complications.  

B. Post‑operative systemic therapy (neoadjuvant for liver disease) – After recovery from the colon resection, give 3–4 cycles of intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because of KRAS mutation and high CEA. Rationale: systemic therapy serves to (i) treat micrometastatic disease, (ii) assess tumor biology (response vs. progression), and (iii) potentially downsize the hepatic lesions, increasing the likelihood of an R0 liver resection.  

C. Re‑assessment of hepatic disease – Repeat high‑quality liver MRI with volumetry after chemotherapy. Confirm that the FLR remains ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight) and that no new extra‑hepatic lesions have appeared. Rationale: ensures that the liver resection remains technically feasible and oncologically justified.  

D. Curative liver resection – Proceed with segmental resection/wedge excision of the metastases in segments II and IVa (or a left‑lateral plus segment IVa resection) aiming for R0 margins, preserving at least two contiguous segments and the middle hepatic vein. Rationale: complete extirpation of all hepatic disease offers the only chance for long‑term survival.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy – Complete the planned total of 12 cycles of chemotherapy (including the pre‑operative cycles) after hepatic surgery, adjusting the regimen based on response and tolerability. Rationale: consolidates systemic control and addresses any residual microscopic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases located in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. MRI confirms preservation of the middle hepatic vein and no major vascular invasion. Both lesions are technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections (in case of effective tumor shrinkage with neoadjuvant therapy) or left hepatectomy with preservation of the middle hepatic vein. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and favorable anatomical location of metastases, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: control of the primary tumor
• The elevated CEA level (95 ng/mL) and right-sided T4N2 colon cancer represents locally advanced disease and is the immediate oncologic priority.
• Given the high CEA level (95 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Assess potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel, duodenum)
• 3 options
-	Perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis, first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications.
-	Perform an derivation ileostomy first to control the primary tumor and prevent local complications during chemotherapy.
-	Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period allows treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Liver surgery after restaging
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan restaging.
• If tumor response is observed on primary cancer : proceed to oncologic right hemicolectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis
• If tumor response is observed on liver metastases, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment II wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy.
• If stability or progression is observed, proceed to anatomic left hepatectomy preserving the middle hepatic vein guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Case_Content:
Man, 47 years old,at the abdominal CT scan T3N0 upper rectal cancer with three liver metastases (segments VI, VII and VIII), sizes 1-2 cm. CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. No other lesions on PET.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases primarily resectable, considered for combined treatment after short-course pelvic radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Technical justification: three metastases 1‑2 cm located in segments VI‑VIII can be removed by limited right‑lobe or non‑anatomic segmental resections; left liver (segments II‑IV) remains intact, providing an estimated future liver remnant >30 % (well above the 20‑30 % safety threshold).  
- Oncologic justification: synchronous disease, ≤3 lesions, each ≤2 cm, no extra‑hepatic disease on PET, RAS wild‑type, and primary staged T3N0 (no nodal involvement). These factors meet current consensus criteria for curative‑intent hepatic resection (ability to achieve R0 margins with adequate FLR).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is resectable. Rationale:  
- Only one hepatic lesion (2.7 cm) located in segment IVb, amenable to an anatomic segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge with negative margins.  
- Technical criteria are satisfied: removal of the lesion would leave >30 % future liver remnant (FLR) and preserve inflow/outflow of at least two contiguous segments.  
- No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease on the thoraco‑abdominal CT.  
- Molecular profile (BRAF wild‑type, MSS) and left‑sided primary are associated with higher resection rates.  
- Patient’s comorbidity (controlled hypertension) does not preclude major abdominal surgery; age 70 alone is not a contraindication if functional status is adequate.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative work‑up (within 2 weeks)  
   • Full performance status assessment (ECOG/ASA), baseline liver function tests, and volumetric CT or MRI to confirm FLR >30 % (or >0.5 % liver‑body‑weight ratio).  
   • Staging of the primary tumor (colonoscopy with biopsy, CT chest, pelvic MRI) to determine T‑stage and nodal status (N).  
   • KRAS/NRAS mutation testing (if not already done).  
   Rationale: ensures patient fitness, confirms absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease, and provides complete oncologic staging.

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional)  
   • If the primary tumor is T3/T4 or N‑positive, or if there is concern about micrometastatic disease, administer 2–3 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑based doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) ± anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab).  
   • For a truly low‑risk biology (small solitary lesion, normal CEA trend, no nodal disease), proceed directly to surgery without pre‑operative chemotherapy.  
   Rationale: peri‑operative chemotherapy can down‑stage occult disease and serves as a “test of time” for tumor biology; however, it is not mandatory for a solitary, resectable metastasis with favorable features.

C. Surgical phase – Simultaneous resection (preferred)  
   • Perform a left‑sided colectomy (segmental resection or hemicolectomy) with oncologic lymphadenectomy.  
   • In the same operation, execute a segment IVb resection (anatomic segmentectomy or wedge) with a ≥5 mm margin, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   • Ensure meticulous hemostasis, bile duct preservation, and adequate FLR perfusion.  
   Rationale: the liver resection is minor (<3 segments), the primary is left‑sided and not obstructed, and simultaneous surgery avoids a second anesthesia, reduces overall treatment time, and has comparable morbidity to staged procedures in this setting.

D. Adjuvant therapy (post‑operative)  
   • Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± biologic) after adequate postoperative recovery (usually 4–6 weeks).  
   • Consider adding targeted therapy based on KRAS/NRAS status (anti‑EGFR if wild‑type).  
   Rationale: adjuvant chemotherapy improves disease‑free survival for resected colorectal liver metastases, especially when high‑risk features (CEA > 30 ng/mL, nodal involvement) are present.

E. Surveillance  
   • CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   • Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually up to 5 years.  
   Rationale: early detection of recurrence allows timely salvage therapies (repeat resection, ablation, or systemic treatment).

   - If primary tumor is asymptomatic and patient is fit: proceed with a liver‑first approach – segmental/wedge resections of segments IV, V, VIII (aiming for R0 margins) preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
   - If primary tumor shows risk of obstruction, perforation, or bleeding: consider colon‑first (left hemicolectomy with en‑bloc resection of any involved adjacent structures) followed by hepatic resection after recovery (≈ 6–8 weeks).  
   - Simultaneous resection may be contemplated only if operative time is acceptable, liver resection is limited (≤ 2 segments), and the patient has no significant comorbidities.  

D. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (additional 6 cycles) tailored to response and tolerability, with continuation of bevacizumab if not contraindicated.  
   - Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT/MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Case_Content:
Man, 49 years old, T2N0 rectal tumor associated with a single 2.8 cm liver metastasis in segment V at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Single metastasis, resectable upfront, surgery considered after local treatment of the primary.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Single hepatic lesion, 2.8 cm, located in segment V – amenable to non‑anatomic wedge resection or segmentectomy with clear (≥1 mm) margins.  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease on the provided CT.  
  • Lesion size <3 cm and solitary meets technical criteria for preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 % in a 70 kg adult).  
  • Primary rectal tumor is T2N0, low stage, not invading adjacent structures; therefore no contraindication to combined surgery.  
  • Patient age (49) and presumed good performance status suggest sufficient physiologic reserve for major abdominal surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging and functional assessment  
   – Obtain chest CT, liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, and high‑resolution pelvic MRI to confirm solitary disease and exclude occult lesions.  
   – Perform liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance (or volumetric CT) to quantify FLR.  
   – Record ASA score, cardiopulmonary evaluation, and baseline CEA.  

B. Neoadjuvant/peri‑operative systemic therapy (optional)  
   – Because the disease is technically resectable and low‑risk, peri‑operative chemotherapy is not mandatory; however, a short course (3–4 cycles) of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) can be offered to treat micrometastatic disease and provide a “test of time.”  
   – If chemotherapy is given, reassess imaging after completion to confirm continued resectability.  

C. Surgical phase – simultaneous resection  
   – Perform minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision for the T2 rectal cancer.  
   – Immediately thereafter, execute a laparoscopic segment V wedge resection/segmentectomy achieving R0 margins; liver resection precedes colorectal resection to minimize blood loss and allow intra‑operative ultrasound confirmation of margins.  
   – Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments and ensure adequate inflow/outflow; no need for portal vein embolization given the small volume resected.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   – Pathology review of both specimens; if margins are negative (R0) and nodes remain N0, proceed with adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (6 months FOLFOX) because KRAS mutation and pre‑operative CEA = 35 ng/mL indicate higher recurrence risk.  
   – Schedule CEA monitoring every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven bilobar liver metastases, sizes 1 to 4 cm at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: vascular contact with the right portal branch.
MDT Discussion: Metastases not resectable upfront, considered for conversion chemotherapy FOLFOX + bevacizumab.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
- Justification:  
  • Seven bilobar metastases (1–4 cm) are technically resectable if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved; current criteria require ≥2 contiguous segments with sufficient inflow/outflow and ≥30 % FLR (or ≥20 % in a healthy liver).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, and liver function tests are stated to be normal, satisfying functional criteria.  
  • Vascular contact with the right portal branch may necessitate limited vascular reconstruction but does not preclude resection.  
  • The number and size of lesions exceed older “four‑lesion” rules, but modern guidelines allow multiple lesions provided an R0 resection and adequate FLR are achievable, especially after down‑staging.  
  • Therefore the disease is not resectable upfront but may become resectable after conversion therapy and/or hypertrophy strategies.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy  
   - Start FOLFOX + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated, anti‑EGFR ineffective).  
   - Give 3–6 cycles (≈12–18 weeks), monitor CEA trend and toxicity.  
   - Rationale: down‑size lesions, test tumor biology, increase likelihood of R0 resection.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment (after 3–4 cycles)  
   - Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase + CT chest/abdomen/pelvis.  
   - Perform 3‑D volumetry to calculate FLR; assess response of each lesion and portal‑branch involvement.  
   - Rationale: determine if sufficient FLR exists or if hypertrophy procedures are needed.  

C. Hypertrophy strategy (if FLR < 30 %)  
   - Options: portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe to be resected, or ALPPS/associating liver partition and portal vein ligation if rapid hypertrophy is required.  
   - Re‑image 2–3 weeks after PVE to confirm FLR growth.  
   - Rationale: create a safe functional remnant before major hepatectomy.  

D. Surgical sequencing  
   - Liver‑first approach (preferred if primary tumor is not obstructing or bleeding):  
        1. Perform definitive hepatic resection aiming for R0 margins (e.g., right posterior sectionectomy + wedge resections of left‑lobe lesions, or staged right hepatectomy after left‑lobe clearance).  
        2. After hepatic recovery (≈4–6 weeks), proceed to extended right hemicolectomy with primary tumor removal.  
   - Simultaneous resection may be considered only if operative risk is low, the primary tumor requires urgent removal, and the planned liver resection is limited (≤3 segments).  
   - Rationale: liver‑first avoids delay of hepatic control and allows assessment of postoperative liver function before a second major operation.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume/continue FOLFOX ± bevacizumab for up to 6 months post‑resection, provided recovery and tolerance.  
   - Serial CEA and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for surveillance.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with seven bilobar liver metastases (1–4 cm) associated with vascular contact with the right portal branch and no reported extrahepatic disease. The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and portal contact make a complete R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant unlikely with an upfront surgical approach. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Given the high CEA level (520 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy with FOLFIRINOX + bevacizumab.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from portal structures, and reduction in the number/volume of lesions to achieve secondary resectability.

C. Early and repeated radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response, particularly the relationship of lesions to the right portal branch and overall liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA dynamics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Consider surgery if chemotherapy induces:
– Reduction in lesion size and number allowing parenchymal-sparing resections or staged hepatectomy or combined resection and ablation.
– Clearance from portal structures.
– Feasibility of achieving R0 resection with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern and tumor location.
• Portal vein embolization may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If no adequate response
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar involvement for conversion, imaging to be re-evaluated after 4 cycles of chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Four bilobar metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) – number and distribution exceed classic “easy” resectability but do not per se preclude surgery if adequate FLR can be preserved.  
  • One lesion contacts the right hepatic vein, threatening outflow; this is a technical limitation that may require vascular reconstruction or R1‑vascular resection, but it is not an absolute contraindication.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; however, the extent of hepatic involvement and the need to preserve at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow remain to be quantified.  
  • High CEA (240 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology, but RAS wild‑type permits effective anti‑EGFR conversion therapy.  
  • Current MDT plan to reassess after 4 cycles of chemotherapy reflects the expectation that systemic therapy can downsize disease and clarify FLR adequacy, consistent with conversion criteria in the literature.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy  
   - Start a 4‑6‑cycle oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) plus anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type; consider adding bevacizumab only if anti‑EGFR contraindicated.  
   - Goal: achieve ≥30 % tumor shrinkage, assess disease biology, and avoid early progression.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (after 4 cycles)  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific agent; obtain volumetric analysis of future liver remnant (FLR).  
   - Measure liver function (ICG‑R15, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count).  
   - If FLR <30 % (or <40 % in steatotic liver), plan right portal vein embolization (PVE) or combined portal vein ligation (PVL) to induce hypertrophy of left lateral sector (segments II‑III).  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   - Option 1 – Two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH)  
     1st stage: Non‑anatomic resection/ablation of left‑lateral lesions (segments II‑III) plus right PVE (or intra‑operative PVL).  
     Interval: 4‑6 weeks, repeat imaging to confirm FLR growth (>30 %).  
     2nd stage: Right hepatectomy (segments VI‑VIII) with careful dissection of the right hepatic vein; if tumor‑vein contact persists, perform R1‑vascular resection or reconstruct the vein as needed.  
   - Option 2 – Single‑stage parenchymal‑sparing resection (if post‑chemotherapy FLR >30 % and margins ≥1 mm can be achieved). Use intra‑operative ultrasound, consider R1‑vascular resection only when margin <1 mm but no macroscopic residual disease.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance phase  
   - Resume systemic therapy (FOLFOX ± cetuximab) for a total of 6 months peri‑operatively.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and cross‑sectional imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years.  
   - Consider liver‑directed local therapy (e.g., intra‑operative ablation of any disappearing lesions) if intra‑operative ultrasound identifies residual disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, and VIII), one of which is in contact with the right hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. The bilobar distribution and venous contact make a complete R0 parenchymal-sparing resection unlikely with an upfront approach while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but not safely resectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all 4 lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (240 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI or FOLFIRINOX) combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status.
• The objective is tumor downsizing, separation from the right hepatic vein, and reduction of bilobar tumor burden to enable secondary resectability.

C. Early radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after 4 cycles as planned to reassess:
– Relationship of the segment VIII lesion to the right hepatic vein.
– Global tumor response and potential for parenchymal-sparing resections.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered if imaging shows:
– Clearance from the right hepatic vein.
– Feasibility of multiple parenchymal-sparing resections or a staged hepatectomy.
– Adequate future liver remnant after planned resections.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Combined parenchymal-sparing resections of segments II, III, VI, and VIII.
• If necessary, a two-stage hepatectomy strategy depending on response pattern and FLR considerations.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Multiple liver metastases (≥8) and size up to 4.5 cm exceed traditional “favorable” numbers but current criteria prioritize ability to achieve an R0 resection rather than absolute lesion count.  
  • Partial contact with the inferior vena cava raises concern for vascular involvement; resection/reconstruction may be required, adding technical complexity.  
  • No data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume; adequacy of FLR is a core technical criterion.  
  • High CEA (890 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology, but BRAF wild‑type is favorable; response to FOLFOXIRI will be used to gauge biological resectability.  
  • Absence of documented extra‑hepatic disease; if none, conversion therapy can render the case resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continuation of conversion chemotherapy  
   - Administer FOLFOXIRI (± anti‑EGFR if KRAS/NRAS wild‑type) for 3–4 months, aiming for ≥30 % radiologic shrinkage or reduction to ≤5 lesions.  
   - Rationale: maximizes chance of converting to resectable status and provides a biological test of tumor aggressiveness.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary agent plus CT volumetry to calculate FLR.  
   - Obtain PET‑CT or chest CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Re‑measure CEA; a falling trend supports favorable biology.  
   - Rationale: precise mapping of disease burden, vascular relationships, and FLR is essential before operative planning.  

C. Pre‑operative liver augmentation if needed  
   - If FLR <30 % (or <0.5 % body weight), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider ALPPS/associating liver partition with staged hepatectomy, depending on liver quality and patient fitness.  
   - Rationale: ensures sufficient postoperative liver function and reduces risk of liver failure.  

D. Surgical sequencing (liver‑first approach)  
   - First stage: curative‑intent liver resection aiming for R0 margins; options include extended right hepatectomy or combined segmental resections with IVC reconstruction if necessary, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound.  
   - Second stage (within 6–8 weeks): definitive resection of the primary left‑sided colon cancer (extended left colectomy) once hepatic recovery is confirmed.  
   - Rationale: prioritizes control of the dominant metastatic burden, minimizes risk of hepatic progression during bowel surgery, and allows assessment of postoperative hepatic reserve before colon surgery.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Resume postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 6 months; consider continuation of anti‑EGFR therapy if KRAS/NRAS wild‑type.  
   - Rationale: eradicates microscopic disease and addresses any residual systemic risk.  

F. Surveillance  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months; imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with extensive bilobar liver metastases (≥8 lesions, up to 4.5 cm) with partial contact with the inferior vena cava and no reported extrahepatic disease. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable upfront, with a possibility of secondary resectability only after major tumor response.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (890 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type and MSS status do not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.

E. Potential surgical strategies if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Preoperative portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy is needed.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Woman, 52 years old, T3N2 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with bilobar liver metastases (six lesions, 2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 600 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: invasion of the middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Not initially resectable, goal of volumetric reduction with chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
   Technical factors – six bilobar metastases (2‑5 cm), invasion of the middle hepatic vein, and likely insufficient future liver remnant (FLR) for an R0 resection with preservation of ≥2 contiguous segments.  
   Oncologic factors – synchronous disease, high CEA (600 ng/mL), KRAS mutation, and N2 nodal status indicate aggressive biology, favoring initial systemic therapy to test disease control (“proof of time”).  
   Current MDT opinion already labels the case as “not initially resectable” with the aim of volumetric reduction, which aligns with the definition of potentially resectable disease that may become resectable after down‑staging and/or hypertrophy strategies.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy  
   - Initiate 4–6 cycles of a doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because KRAS is mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated).  
   - Rationale: high tumor burden and need for rapid down‑staging; bevacizumab improves response rates and may facilitate later resection.  

B. Early radiologic reassessment (2–3 months)  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with volumetric analysis; repeat CEA; assess RECIST response and calculate FLR.  
   - Rationale: determine whether sufficient tumor shrinkage and FLR (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % after chemotherapy) have been achieved to allow a safe hepatectomy.

   - Continue systemic therapy during the hypertrophy interval (typically 2–4 weeks).  
   - Rationale: augment FLR to meet the 30 % (or 40 % after chemotherapy) threshold while maintaining disease control.

   - Clear all metastases in the future liver remnant (usually left lateral segments) using non‑anatomic resections or intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided ablation.  
   - Rationale: achieve R0 clearance of the FLR before the major resection, preserving maximal functional liver tissue.

   - After confirmed FLR hypertrophy (typically 4–6 weeks post‑PVE) perform right hepatectomy (or extended right hepatectomy) to remove remaining lesions, ensuring negative margins and adequate inflow/outflow.  
   - Rationale: completes curative‑intent hepatic clearance while respecting technical resectability criteria.

   - If not already given, deliver long‑course chemoradiotherapy (or short‑course radiotherapy followed by consolidation chemotherapy) during the hepatic treatment interval.  
   - Follow with total mesorectal excision (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection as dictated by tumor response and sphincter involvement).  
   - Rationale: synchronous rectal cancer requires definitive local control; a “liver‑first” sequence avoids delay of hepatic curative intent.

   - Post‑operative FOLFOX (± bevacizumab) for 6 months, adjusted to postoperative recovery and liver function.  
   - Rationale: consolidates disease control, addresses micrometastatic risk, and follows evidence from peri‑operative trials.

- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline) after conversion  
- Justification:  
  • Nine bilobar metastases exceed the traditional “≤4 lesions” cutoff and are located close to major hepatic veins, making an R0 resection technically challenging.  
  • Preservation of ≥2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage is unlikely without substantial liver volume reduction; current imaging suggests insufficient future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • High tumor burden (CEA 950 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive biology, but do not preclude conversion.  
  • According to contemporary criteria, patients who cannot achieve an R0 resection now but may do so after downsizing with systemic therapy are deemed “potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an oxaliplatin‑based triplet (FOLFOXIRI) plus bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) for 4–6 cycles (KRAS‑mutated disease excludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
   - Rationale: highest reported response rates (>50 %) in KRAS‑mutated mCRC; provides both tumor downsizing and a test of disease biology.

   - Repeat contrast‑enhanced liver MRI and triphasic CT; measure FLR (volumetry) and assess response (RECIST, CEA trend).  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (healthy liver) or ≥ 40 % (post‑chemotherapy liver) and margins appear achievable → proceed to surgery.  
   - If FLR remains inadequate, plan a hypertrophy strategy:  
        • Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments to be resected, or  
        • Liver venous deprivation (LVD) if rapid hypertrophy is needed, or  
        • Two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) with first‑stage clearance of the future liver remnant followed by PVE.  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   - Liver‑first approach (preferred because primary tumor is not reported as obstructive or bleeding).  
        • Perform parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy aiming for R0; if lesions abut hepatic veins, consider R1 vascular resection or limited vascular reconstruction, which is acceptable in KRAS‑mutated disease when FLR is adequate.  
        • Use intra‑operative ultrasound to locate any disappearing lesions; consider fiducial markers placed before chemotherapy for guidance.  
   - Primary tumor resection after hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks later).  
        • Standard right hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy (aim for ≥12 nodes).  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume the same systemic regimen (or switch to FOLFIRI + bevacizumab if toxicity limits) for an additional 6 months post‑operatively, provided R0/R1 resection is achieved and the patient recovers adequately.  
   - Continue surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years.

  • Largest lesion 5.5 cm (size >5 cm is an unfavorable oncologic factor).  
  • High pre‑operative CEA (800 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive biology.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease reported on the current CT, satisfying the oncologic criterion that limited extra‑hepatic disease does not preclude resection.  
  • Ability to preserve at least two contiguous liver segments and achieve adequate vascular inflow/outflow is uncertain without volumetric data; therefore, conversion to resectability will likely require hypertrophy strategies (PVE/ALPPS) and systemic down‑staging.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start a doublet or triplet regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   - Rationale: down‑size lesions, test tumor biology, and improve the chance of an R0 resection; anti‑EGFR agents are avoided because of KRAS mutation.

   - Perform contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT, PET‑CT if needed, and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume.

   - If FLR is <30 % of total liver volume, embolize the portal branches feeding the lobe that will be resected first (typically the right lobe).

   - Resect all metastases located in the future liver remnant (e.g., left lateral section) or perform limited resection of lesions in the non‑embolized lobe, combined with PVE if not already done.

E. Interval reassessment (4–6 weeks)  
   - Repeat volumetry and imaging to confirm FLR growth (>30 %) and absence of progression.  
   - Rationale: ensure safe hepatic reserve before the second, more extensive operation.

   - Perform right (or left) hepatectomy to remove the remaining metastases, aiming for R0 margins while preserving the hypertrophied FLR.  
   - Rationale: achieve complete extirpation of all hepatic disease.  

G. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary is asymptomatic, schedule a definitive left‑sided colectomy after hepatic clearance (within 4–6 weeks).  
   - If obstructive or symptomatic, consider simultaneous colon resection during the first stage or a “liver‑first” approach with early colon surgery after hepatic clearance, depending on intra‑operative findings and patient condition.  

H. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Resume or modify chemotherapy post‑operatively based on pathological response, margin status, and nodal stage (T3N2).

Woman, 50 years old, T3N1M1 rectal cancer, five liver metastases (segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII), max size 4.1 cm. CEA 370 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Extensive bilobar involvement, possibility of conversion depending on response to chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Five bilobar metastases, each ≤4.1 cm, meet technical criteria for R0 resection if adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved (≥30 % in a normal liver, ≥40 % after chemotherapy).  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; therefore, disease is not excluded on oncologic grounds.  
  • KRAS mutation and markedly elevated CEA (370 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology but are not absolute contraindications; they support the need for a conversion strategy and careful postoperative surveillance.  
  • The number of lesions (5) and bilobar distribution preclude a single‑stage major hepatectomy without risking insufficient FLR, making a staged or parenchymal‑sparing approach necessary.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Conversion systemic therapy  
   – Initiate 3–4 months of intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status).  
   – Goal: achieve ≥30 % reduction in total tumor volume, assess tumor biology (“proof of time”), and avoid chemotherapy‑induced liver injury by limiting cycles to ≤6.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with liver volumetry, PET‑CT to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease, and calculate FLR.  
   – If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % after chemotherapy) and all lesions are resectable with negative margins, proceed to surgery; if FLR insufficient, plan hypertrophy.  

C. Surgical plan (liver‑first approach)  
   – Option 1: Two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) – first stage clears lesions in the future liver remnant (segments II/III/IV), followed by right‑portal vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy, then second‑stage right hepatectomy.  
   – Option 2: Parenchymal‑sparing non‑anatomic resections combined with intra‑operative ablation (RFA/MWA) for lesions adjacent to major vessels, aiming for R0 resection while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
   – Choose the approach that yields adequate FLR and R0 margins with the lowest morbidity.  

D. Management of the primary rectal tumor  
   – If not already resected, schedule total mesorectal excision (TME) after hepatic recovery (typically 6–8 weeks).  
   – Provide short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) pre‑operatively if not given, especially given T3 stage.  
   – Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy for 6 months, tailored to pathology and response, to address micrometastatic disease.

Man, 62 years old, operated 4 years ago for right colon adenocarcinoma (T3N1M0), no initial recurrence. Surveillance: CEA 180 ng/mL. At the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: two liver lesions segments V and VIII, 2.8 and 3.2 cm. Liver MRI confirms no other foci. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metachronous metastases, anatomically accessible, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable (not merely potentially resectable).  
- Technical factors supporting resectability:  
  • Two discrete lesions (2.8 cm in segment V, 3.2 cm in segment VIII) amenable to segmental resection or limited right hepatectomy.  
  • Expected future liver remnant >30 % of total liver volume, satisfying the ≥30 % FLR rule.  
  • No radiologic evidence of vascular invasion, biliary obstruction, or multifocal bilobar disease.  
- Biological/clinical factors supporting curative intent:  
  • Metachronous presentation (4 years after primary resection) – associated with better outcomes than synchronous disease.  
  • No extra‑hepatic metastases on thoraco‑abdominal CT and liver MRI.  
  • Patient described as in “good general condition” (presumed ECOG 0‑1).  
  • KRAS mutation is a negative prognostic marker but does not preclude resection; BRAF wild‑type further supports feasibility.  
  • CEA markedly elevated (180 ng/mL) – high but not an absolute contraindication; can be used for postoperative surveillance.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Confirm disease extent  
   – Obtain repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and a chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease and to reassess lesion size/vascular relationships.  
   – Calculate volumetric future liver remnant (CT‑based or MRI‑based).  

B. Surgical intervention (first‑line)  
   – Proceed to curative‑intent liver resection aiming for R0 margins.  
   – Preferred operation: limited right hepatectomy or combined segment V + VIII resection, preserving ≥30 % FLR.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and detect any additional sub‑centimeter metastases.  

C. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   – Given KRAS mutation and high CEA, administer adjuvant chemotherapy after surgery (e.g., 3–6 months of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab).  
   – Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is optional; if there is any uncertainty about tumor biology, a short (2‑3 month) pre‑operative FOLFOX regimen can be given to obtain “proof of time” and assess response before resection.  

D. Post‑operative surveillance  
   – CEA every 2–3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   – Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest CT every 6 months for the first 3 years, then annually.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.

   No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease; prior rectal resection was curative and there is no current rectal lesion.  
   RAS wild‑type, MSS – favorable biology for surgical cure.  
   Technical criteria (adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage, FLR) are satisfied based on the described lesion locations.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (3–4 cycles of FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody).  
   - Rationale: high pre‑operative CEA (95 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; pre‑operative chemotherapy provides “proof of time,” allows CEA trend monitoring, and may down‑size the micronodule if needed.  

B. Restaging after chemotherapy (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI ± CT, repeat CEA).  
   - Rationale: confirm disease stability or response, ensure no new lesions, and re‑calculate FLR volume.  

C. Curative liver resection (left lateral segmentectomy + wedge resection of segment V).  
   - Rationale: achieves R0 resection of all known disease with adequate margins; avoids major hepatectomy, limits operative risk in a 70‑year‑old.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy (completion of 6 months total peri‑operative chemotherapy).  
   - Rationale: high‑risk features (node‑positive primary, elevated CEA) merit postoperative chemotherapy to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  

E. Surveillance (CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging of liver and chest every 6 months for at least 3 years).  
   - Rationale: early detection of recurrence, which is common after hepatic resection.

- Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
- Justification:  
  • Four hepatic metastases (1.5‑3.5 cm) exceed the historic “< 4 lesions” rule but current criteria prioritize the ability to achieve an R0 resection with preservation of ≥ 2 contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver).

  • Lack of information on lesion distribution (unilateral vs bilateral), proximity to major vessels, and baseline liver function prevents a definitive “resectable” label; therefore the case is considered potentially resectable pending further technical assessment (volumetry, vascular anatomy) and biological assessment (response to systemic therapy).

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and technical assessment  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and three‑dimensional volumetric analysis.  
   - Determine FLR volume, lesion topography (segmental location, bilobar vs unilobar), and relationship to hepatic veins/portal pedicles.  
   - Review liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin), indocyanine‑green clearance if available, and patient performance status (ECOG/ASA).  

B. Systemic induction therapy  
   - Initiate 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles) of modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) or triplet (FOLFOXIRI) if tolerated, given the high‑risk primary (T4 N2) and KRAS‑mutated biology.  
   - Aim to (i) assess tumor biology (stability vs progression) and (ii) potentially downsize lesions to facilitate a less extensive hepatectomy.  
   - Re‑image after chemotherapy to document response and re‑evaluate resectability.  

C. Surgical plan (curative intent)  
   - If lesions are confined to one lobe and FLR ≥ 30 %: proceed with a single‑stage anatomical or non‑anatomical resection (segmentectomy/partial hepatectomy) aiming for R0 margins; consider intra‑operative ultrasound and, when needed, adjunctive radiofrequency ablation for deep or marginal lesions.  
   - If lesions are bilateral and FLR would be insufficient: adopt a staged approach:  
        • First stage – clear metastases from the future remnant liver (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy or limited resections) and perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased lobe to induce hypertrophy.  
        • Interval of 4–6 weeks with repeat imaging to confirm FLR growth (> 30 %).  
        • Second stage – resect the hypertrophied remnant‑lobe disease (right hepatectomy or extended resection).  
   - If rapid hypertrophy is required and patient fitness permits: consider ALPPS (partial) as an alternative, recognizing higher morbidity and the need for careful selection.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy for 3–6 months post‑resection (same regimen if tolerated, or switch to a different backbone if progression occurred).  
   - Follow‑up schedule: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually; PET‑CT if CEA rises or imaging is equivocal.

Case_Content:
Woman, 71 years old, left colon cancer operated 5 years ago. Liver MRI: liver lesion segment V, 2.8 cm. CEA 90 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, favorable context, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Single hepatic metastasis, 2.8 cm, located in segment V – amenable to a non‑anatomic segmentectomy or wedge resection.  
  • Technical criteria for resectability are met: removal of the lesion would preserve at least two contiguous liver segments (the remaining left lateral and right posterior sectors), maintain vascular inflow/outflow and biliary drainage, and leave a future liver remnant (FLR) well above the minimum 30 % (estimated FLR > 70 % given solitary lesion).  
  • No radiologic evidence of extra‑hepatic disease on the provided MRI; MDT notes “isolated metastasis.”  
  • Patient is described as having good general condition, implying adequate performance status and organ reserve.  
  • RAS wild‑type status does not preclude surgery and supports eligibility for anti‑EGFR‑containing systemic regimens if needed.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging – obtain contrast‑enhanced chest CT (or PET‑CT) and a full liver CT/MRI volumetric study to confirm absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease and to quantify FLR precisely.  
   • Rationale: ensures true liver‑only disease and validates that the FLR is sufficient; aligns with oncologic criteria that require complete R0 resection of all known disease.  

B. Upfront hepatic resection – perform a segment V anatomical/non‑anatomical resection with a goal of R0 margin (≥1 mm, preferably ≥5 mm).  
   • Rationale: solitary, technically resectable lesion in a fit patient; upfront surgery avoids delay and provides the best chance for cure.  

C. Adjuvant systemic therapy – initiate 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody such as cetuximab, given RAS wild‑type) beginning within 6–8 weeks post‑op once recovery is adequate.  
   • Rationale: high pre‑operative CEA (90 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; adjuvant chemotherapy reduces micrometastatic risk and is supported by EORTC 40983 and subsequent data.  

D. Surveillance – follow with CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest imaging at 6‑month intervals for at least 3 years.  
   • Rationale: early detection of recurrence improves eligibility for repeat curative interventions (re‑resection, ablation).
