Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, history of rectal resection (T3N1) 2 years ago. Liver MRI: two liver metastases, segments II and VIII, 2.5 and 3 cm. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 240 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, technically accessible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Technical assessment: Two isolated metastases (2.5 cm in segment II, 3 cm in segment VIII) are amenable to non‑anatomic or segmental resections; the remaining liver volume is expected to exceed the 30 % future liver remnant threshold, and vascular inflow/outflow can be preserved.  
- Oncologic assessment: Metachronous recurrence (2 years after primary surgery) is favorable, but the patient has a high pre‑operative CEA (240 ng/mL > 200 ng/mL) and a KRAS mutation, both recognized adverse prognostic factors. No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on thoracic CT.  
- Classification: Technically resectable but with unfavorable biological markers → potentially resectable / borderline. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy is recommended before definitive liver surgery to obtain “proof of time” and improve disease‑free survival.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (3–4 months)  
   - Regimen: oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) plus bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF), avoiding anti‑EGFR agents because of KRAS mutation.  
   - Rationale: down‑size lesions if needed, treat occult micrometastases, and assess tumor biology through radiologic response.  

B. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) with volumetric analysis of the future liver remnant.  
   - Rationale: confirm that both lesions remain resectable and that FLR is adequate; identify any new lesions or progression.  

C. Surgical resection (if restaging confirms resectability)  
   - Perform simultaneous, non‑major hepatectomy: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment VIII wedge/segmentectomy, preserving ≥30 % liver volume.  
   - No need for portal vein embolization given the limited extent.  
   - Rationale: curative‑intent R0 resection achievable with low operative risk; simultaneous approach avoids a second operation and shortens overall treatment time.  

D. Adjuvant/peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Resume or continue the same chemotherapy regimen for an additional 2–3 months post‑operatively to complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative therapy, or switch to a different doublet if resistance is suspected.  
   - Rationale: consolidates the benefit of neoadjuvant treatment, addresses microscopic disease, and aligns with guideline‑based peri‑operative chemotherapy for CRLM.  

If restaging shows progression or insufficient FLR, consider alternative strategies such as portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy, or local ablative modalities (RFA/SBRT) before attempting resection.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab there is a 60 % volumetric reduction and CEA falls from 880 ng/mL to 180 ng/mL, indicating good biologic response.  
  • Imaging now shows 5 residual liver lesions that are well‑defined and bilobar, a number that can be addressed with parenchymal‑sparing resections provided adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported on the available work‑up, satisfying the oncologic requirement for an R0 resection of all known disease.  
  • Technical criteria for resectability (preservation of at least two contiguous hepatic segments, maintenance of inflow/outflow and biliary drainage) cannot be confirmed without FLR volumetry and assessment of vascular proximity; therefore the case remains “potentially” rather than definitively resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Complete conversion chemotherapy – administer 2–4 additional cycles of the same regimen (FOLFOX + bevacizumab) or switch to a short course of FOLFIRI if toxicity emerges, aiming to maximize tumor shrinkage while limiting total pre‑operative cycles to ≤8 to avoid chemotherapy‑induced liver injury.  
B. Comprehensive restaging – obtain:  
   • Triple‑phase contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   • Gd‑EOB‑MRI with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (normal liver) or <40 % (chemotherapy‑injured liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage/ALPPS approach.  
   • Laboratory assessment: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, indocyanine‑green clearance, and assessment of chemotherapy‑related hepatotoxicity (sinusoidal injury, steatohepatitis).  
C. Surgical plan –  
   • If FLR is adequate, proceed with a one‑stage, parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy (multiple non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmental resections) targeting all 5 lesions with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance, aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm) or R1 vascular resection if necessary.  
   • Decide on timing of primary tumor resection: if the primary is asymptomatic and patient’s performance status permits, perform simultaneous left‑sided colectomy (or anterior resection) with liver surgery; if not, schedule staged approach (primary first → liver, or reverse liver‑first) based on symptomatology and FLR considerations.  
D. Post‑operative oncologic management –  
   • Resume systemic therapy within 6–8 weeks after liver surgery, completing a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (pre‑ + post‑operative).  
   • Consider continuation of bevacizumab in the adjuvant phase if no wound‑healing complications and if the primary tumor has been resected with clear margins.  
   • Enroll patient in a structured surveillance program (CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging at 6‑month intervals) for early detection of recurrence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, the patient shows a major radiologic and biologic response (≈60% volumetric reduction; CEA from 880 to 180 ng/mL). MRI now demonstrates five well-defined residual liver lesions without reported extrahepatic disease. In this context of marked downsizing and clearer lesion delineation, a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant appears potentially achievable. This pattern is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Immediate high-quality restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to reassess precise segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships after tumor shrinkage.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical conversion strategy
• If imaging confirms feasibility, proceed to parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of all five lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may be performed as a single-stage or staged hepatectomy.
• The goal is complete clearance of residual disease while preserving maximal functional parenchyma.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic chemotherapy after recovery to complete a total of approximately 6 months of treatment (including preoperative cycles).

E. Surveillance
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Eight bilobar metastases exceed the traditional “≤4 lesions” cut‑off, making upfront R0 resection technically challenging.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on thoracic CT, preserving the possibility of a curative intent liver‑first approach.  
  • Imaging after 4 months of FOLFIRI shows disease stability (no progression, no shrinkage) and CEA remains markedly elevated (420 ng/mL), indicating biologically aggressive disease and insufficient tumor response to date.  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) volume and hepatic functional reserve are not provided; without this data a definitive technical resectability cannot be confirmed.  
  • According to current criteria, patients with multiple bilobar lesions who have not demonstrated a radiologic response are considered “borderline” and may become resectable after further effective systemic therapy and/or hypertrophy strategies (PVE, two‑stage hepatectomy, ALPPS).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Optimise systemic therapy – Switch to a more intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab or, if RAS wild‑type, add anti‑EGFR therapy). Rationale: achieve tumor shrinkage and assess disease biology; conversion rates are higher with triplet or doublet plus targeted agents.  
B. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) with volumetry, measure FLR, and obtain RECIST response and CEA trend. Rationale: determine whether sufficient downsizing and FLR adequacy have been achieved to permit curative surgery.  
C. Conversion to resectability (if response achieved) –  
   • If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % with chemotherapy‑associated liver injury) and all lesions can be cleared with negative margins, plan a parenchymal‑sparing, staged hepatectomy (e.g., right‑portal vein embolisation followed by right‑hepatectomy, or two‑stage hepatectomy with segmental resections).  
   • If FLR remains insufficient, consider ALPPS or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy.  
   Rationale: achieve an R0 liver resection while preserving adequate hepatic function.  
D. Primary tumour management –  
   • If the primary sigmoid tumour has not been resected and the patient is asymptomatic, schedule either a simultaneous limited liver resection with primary resection (if FLR and operative time allow) or a staged approach (primary resection first, then liver surgery).  
   Rationale: avoid postoperative complications related to combined major procedures; prioritize curative intent for both sites.  
E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy – Resume or continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months total peri‑operative therapy) tailored to molecular profile. Rationale: eradicate microscopic disease and improve disease‑free survival.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.
MDT Discussion: Partial response, evaluation of segmental resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Justification:  
   Initial burden of ten liver metastases has been reduced to seven detectable lesions after FOLFOXIRI, with three lesions disappearing and the remaining showing a ≥40 % size reduction and hypo‑intense signal on MRI, indicating a favorable biological response.  
   No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the extent of hepatic involvement (segmental distribution, proximity to major vessels, and future liver remnant volume) has not been quantified; therefore technical feasibility cannot be confirmed.  
   Current oncologic criteria (ability to achieve R0 resection, control of disease on systemic therapy) are met in principle, but the technical criteria (preservation of ≥2 contiguous segments, adequate inflow/outflow, and sufficient FLR) remain unevaluated. Hence the case is not yet clearly resectable but is convertible with further assessment and possible adjuncts (PVE, two‑stage approach).

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Continue systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI ± biologic agent appropriate to molecular profile).  
   - Rationale: consolidate tumor response, further downsize lesions, and use response as a biological test of disease aggressiveness before committing to surgery.  

B. Comprehensive restaging (within 4–6 weeks of the last chemotherapy cycle):  
   - Multiphasic contrast‑enhanced MRI with hepatobiliary contrast for precise lesion mapping and volumetric analysis of future liver remnant (FLR).  
   - CT chest/abdomen‑pelvis or PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Laboratory panel: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, and assessment for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
   - Rationale: determine technical resectability, FLR adequacy, and confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Surgical planning based on restaging results  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume in a healthy liver (or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑injured) and all residual lesions can be cleared with negative margins while preserving vascular inflow/outflow, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection (potentially a staged or extended hepatectomy).  
   - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  
   - Rationale: achieve an R0 resection while minimizing risk of post‑hepatectomy liver failure.  

D. Management of the rectal primary  
   - If not already treated, deliver neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the rectal tumor after hepatic surgery (or concurrently if patient fitness allows).  
   - Follow with definitive rectal resection (low anterior resection or appropriate sphincter‑preserving procedure) once the patient has recovered from hepatic surgery.  
   - Complete the course with adjuvant systemic therapy (continuation of FOLFOXIRI or a maintenance regimen) to address micrometastatic disease.  
   - Rationale: coordinated treatment of both sites maximizes oncologic control and functional outcomes.  

E. If resection remains infeasible after restaging:  
   - Consider local ablative modalities (RFA, microwave ablation, or stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual liver lesions.  
   - Continue systemic therapy and reassess periodically.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After FOLFOXIRI, three lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions show ~40% reduction, with several becoming hypo-intense on MRI. Despite this favorable response, the initial tumor burden and presumed bilobar distribution make immediate R0 resection uncertain without precise segmental mapping and volumetric assessment. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging before any decision
• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Assessment of true segmental resectability
• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.
• Intra-operative ultrasound will be essential to localize occult residual disease.

C. Surgical strategy if complete clearance is feasible
• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
   Technical factors: only two metastases located in segments VII and VIII; a right posterior sectionectomy (or limited right hepatectomy) could achieve an R0 resection while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments.  
   Functional factors: no data on future liver remnant (FLR) volume, but assuming no diffuse liver disease, a limited resection is likely to leave an adequate FLR (>30 %).  
   Oncologic/biologic factors: disease has progressed after 8 cycles of optimal FOLFOX, indicating aggressive tumor biology; current guidelines advise deferring surgery until disease control is demonstrated with second‑line systemic therapy.  
   No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the high CEA (950 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation further support a need for systemic disease control before operative intervention.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Second‑line systemic therapy  
   - Initiate FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) given KRAS‑mutated status; aim for disease stabilization or response.  
   - Rationale: progression on first‑line oxaliplatin‑based regimen necessitates a change in chemotherapy backbone; anti‑VEGF improves response rates and may increase conversion to resectability.  

B. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months of second‑line therapy  
   - Perform triphasic CT or MRI with volumetric analysis to:  
     • Evaluate tumor response (size reduction or stability).  
     • Calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).  
   - Rationale: confirmation of disease control and adequate hepatic reserve are prerequisites for curative surgery.  

C. Curative‑intent hepatic resection (if criteria met)  
   - Proceed with right posterior sectionectomy (segments VII‑VIII) or extended right hepatectomy, ensuring negative margins (R0) and preservation of inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   - Rationale: removal of all viable hepatic disease offers the only chance for long‑term survival; limited anatomic resection minimizes loss of functional liver parenchyma.  

D. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume the same systemic regimen (FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) for 6 months as adjuvant therapy, provided postoperative recovery is adequate.  
   - Consider enrollment in a clinical trial (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion pump, Y‑90 radioembolisation) if further disease control is needed.  
   - Rationale: adjuvant systemic therapy consolidates the surgical benefit and addresses micrometastatic disease; targeted approaches may improve outcomes in KRAS‑mutated mCRC.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (converted from initially unresectable).  
- Justification:  
  • Initial burden was seven liver metastases, now four have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have shrunk, indicating a major tumor response.  
  • Normalized CEA and good systemic response suggest favorable tumor biology.  
  • Current imaging shows residual disease in only a few segments; assuming the remaining lesions are amenable to an R0 resection and that at least two contiguous liver segments can be preserved, the technical criteria for resection are met.  
  • Oncologic criteria require removal of all disease, including the sites of the lesions that have disappeared, because microscopic persistence is common; therefore the case is not yet resectable without further surgical planning, placing it in the “potentially resectable” category.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT) and compare with baseline pre‑chemotherapy imaging to map the exact locations of the four lesions that have disappeared.  
   - Perform a volumetric CT‑based calculation of future liver remnant (FLR); target ≥30 % of total liver volume in a liver previously exposed to oxaliplatin‑based chemotherapy (or ≥0.5 % of body weight).  
   - Rationale: precise anatomical mapping is essential for planning parenchymal‑sparing resections and for confirming that the FLR is adequate.  

B. Surgical planning – liver  
   - Plan a parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy that removes all radiologically visible metastases and includes anatomical resection (segmentectomy or subsegmentectomy) of the original sites of the four lesions that have disappeared, guided intra‑operatively by ultrasound and the pre‑treatment imaging overlay.  
   - Ensure negative macroscopic margins (R0) and preservation of at least two contiguous functional segments with intact inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage.  
   - If FLR is borderline, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage approach before definitive resection.  
   - Rationale: microscopic disease is present in most “disappearing” sites; resection of those areas reduces recurrence risk and aligns with oncologic standards.  

C. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - If the primary left‑sided colon cancer is resectable and the patient’s performance status permits, perform a simultaneous extended left colectomy (or segmental resection) with the liver operation.  
   - If operative risk is high or extensive liver work is required, adopt a staged approach (colon first, then liver after recovery).  
   - Rationale: simultaneous resection shortens overall treatment time and avoids a second laparotomy when feasible; staging is reserved for high‑risk patients.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX) ± panitumumab for a total of 6 months (including the pre‑operative cycles) as adjuvant treatment.  
   - Monitor CEA and cross‑sectional imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years.  
   - Rationale: peri‑operative chemotherapy improves disease‑free survival and addresses micrometastatic disease that may remain after resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, four lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have significantly decreased in size, with normalization of CEA. Despite this excellent response, the initial tumor burden and the phenomenon of “disappearing metastases” mean that viable microscopic disease may persist at the original sites. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but requires meticulous mapping of all initial metastatic locations before surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and systematically compare with pre-treatment imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy addressing initial disease map
• Plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided surgical approach that includes resection or ablation of all initial metastatic locations, not only residual visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to identify occult residual disease.
• Depending on lesion distribution, this may require a staged approach.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete surgical clearance of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • After 4 cycles of systemic therapy the liver MRI shows only three residual lesions, each <2 cm, indicating a major radiologic response.  
  • Current oncologic criteria accept any number of lesions provided an R0 resection can be achieved with an adequate future liver remnant (≥20‑30 % of total liver volume).  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease has been reported; absence of such disease removes a major oncologic contraindication.  
  • The initial burden (10 lesions) was high, so the case remains “potentially” rather than unequivocally “resectable” until technical feasibility (lesion location, FLR volume) is confirmed.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform high‑resolution hepatobiliary MRI with volumetric analysis, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen, and PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).  
   - Rationale: definitive assessment of oncologic and technical resectability before committing to surgery.  

B. Multidisciplinary decision & optimization  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or FLR/body‑weight ratio > 0.5) and no extra‑hepatic disease, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy to hypertrophy the remnant.  
   - Rationale: ensures safe hepatic reserve and maximizes chance of R0 resection.  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   - Liver‑first approach (preferred when the rectal primary is asymptomatic and no urgent need for pelvic control):  
        • Perform anatomical or non‑anatomical resection of the three lesions with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance, aiming for ≥1 mm negative margin (R0).  
        • Preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   - Rectal primary management: after hepatic recovery (≈4‑6 weeks), deliver standard neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for the rectal tumor followed by total mesorectal excision (TME) or consider simultaneous liver‑first + TME if operative risk acceptable.  
   - Rationale: liver‑first minimizes risk of chemotherapy‑induced liver injury before major hepatectomy and addresses the disease with the best chance of cure first.  

D. Adjuvant systemic therapy & surveillance  
   - Resume/continue systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) for at least 3‑6 months post‑operatively; given RAS‑wild‑type status, add anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody if not previously used.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Rationale: eradicates microscopic disease, leverages the “proof of time” concept, and enables early detection of recurrence.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Technical criteria for hepatic resection (ability to preserve ≥2 contiguous segments, adequate inflow/outflow, and an FLR ≥ 30% of total liver volume) are not documented; therefore a definitive technical assessment cannot be made.  
  • Oncologic criteria: the patient has T4N2 primary disease, CEA = 600 ng/mL, and has developed new metastatic lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression and an unfavorable biology. Progression on optimal first‑line chemotherapy is a negative prognostic factor and generally contraindicates immediate surgery.  
  • Bilobar distribution of metastases further challenges a single‑stage curative resection, but modern strategies (portal vein embolization, two‑stage hepatectomy, ALPPS, parenchymal‑sparing surgery) can convert selected patients.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease (e.g., lung, peritoneum) is reported; if present, it would shift the classification toward unresectable.  
  • In the absence of clear FLR data and given limited response, the case remains potentially resectable pending further systemic control and detailed volumetric assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Optimize systemic therapy  
   - Switch to a more intensive conversion regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type, or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab if RAS‑mutated).  
   - Rationale: higher response rates (>50 %) increase the likelihood of down‑staging bilobar disease and provide a “test‑of‑time” to assess tumor biology.  

B. Comprehensive restaging after 2–3 months  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT with liver protocol) plus chest CT/PET to evaluate: number, size, distribution of hepatic lesions, appearance of new extra‑hepatic sites, and calculate FLR volume.  
   - Rationale: precise imaging is essential to determine technical resectability and to detect occult disease that would preclude curative surgery.  

C. Conversion/augmentation plan if disease control achieved  
   - If ≥ 70 % of lesions are resectable and FLR is < 30 % but ≥ 25 %: consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or liver venous deprivation to induce hypertrophy.  
   - If disease remains bilobar with insufficient FLR after PVE, evaluate a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) or ALPPS (only in highly selected patients with good performance status).  
   - Rationale: these strategies expand the pool of patients who can undergo an R0 liver resection while preserving adequate liver function.  

D. Surgical phase  
   - Once hepatic disease is down‑staged and FLR is adequate, proceed with curative intent surgery:  
     • Primary tumor: extended right colectomy with oncologic lymphadenectomy (addressing T4 disease).  
     • Liver: parenchymal‑sparing resections of all remaining metastases (aim for R0; R1 vascular resection acceptable in selected cases).  
   - Decide between simultaneous versus staged resection based on operative risk (major hepatectomy + colectomy) and liver remnant size; staged approach is preferred when major hepatectomy is required.  
   - Rationale: achieving complete macroscopic clearance of both intra‑ and extra‑hepatic disease offers the only chance for long‑term survival.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases with the appearance of two new lesions while on FOLFOX, indicating disease progression under systemic therapy. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution, and ongoing progression make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The appearance of new lesions under FOLFOX indicates resistance to the current regimen.
• A change of systemic protocol is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± targeted therapy depending on molecular profile).
• The objective is to regain disease control and potentially create a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 61 years old, left colon cancer, KRAS mutated. Ten initial liver metastases. After chemotherapy: three lesions not visualized, six stable, one progressing (segment VII, 5 cm) at the abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Heterogeneous response, feasibility of selective local treatment to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is potentially resectable.  
- Current imaging shows 7 viable liver metastases (6 stable, 1 progressing, 5 cm in segment VII).  
- Technical resectability criteria (ability to achieve R0 margins, preserve ≥20‑30 % future liver remnant with adequate inflow/outflow) cannot be confirmed without data on lesion distribution, proximity to major vessels, and volumetric liver reserve.  
- Oncologic criteria: no documented extra‑hepatic disease, primary tumor status unknown, KRAS‑mutated (predicts poorer response to EGFR‑targeted agents but does not preclude surgery).  
- Heterogeneous response after systemic therapy suggests that disease biology is not uniformly aggressive, supporting a “borderline/potentially resectable” classification pending further evaluation.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging (2–3 weeks)  
   • Perform triphasic contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with liver‑specific contrast, and PET‑CT to confirm the number, size, exact location of all hepatic lesions and to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   • Calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume; assess vascular anatomy (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery) and biliary drainage.  
   • Review performance status, comorbidities, liver function tests, and baseline tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9).  

B. Systemic therapy optimisation (4–6 weeks)  
   • If the progressing 5 cm lesion is deemed borderline resectable, switch to a second‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) because KRAS mutation precludes anti‑EGFR antibodies.  
   • Continue systemic therapy for 2–3 months (“test‑of‑time”) to assess disease kinetics; aim for disease stability or further shrinkage of the progressing lesion.  

C. Local‑regional control of the progressing lesion (concurrent with B)  
   • Consider image‑guided ablative therapy (RFA or microwave) or stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) for the segment VII lesion if it remains >2 cm after systemic therapy and is technically amenable, thereby converting the patient to a resectable state while preserving FLR.  

D. Re‑assessment of resectability (after 2–3 months of combined systemic + local therapy)  
   • Multidisciplinary review of updated imaging and FLR calculation.  
   • If FLR is adequate, plan curative‑intent hepatic resection aiming for R0 margins of all lesions.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, employ portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy before definitive resection.  

E. Surgical phase  
   • Perform liver‑first (reverse) approach if major hepatectomy is required and the primary colon tumor is asymptomatic; otherwise consider simultaneous resection if the primary is resectable and the hepatic operation is limited.  
   • Aim for negative margins (≥1 mm) and preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow.  

F. Post‑operative management  
   • Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (same regimen if tolerated) for 3–6 months as adjuvant therapy.  
   • Surveillance with 3‑month imaging for the first year, then 6‑month intervals, monitoring CEA and clinical status.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had ten liver metastases. After chemotherapy, three lesions are no longer visualized, six remain stable, and one lesion in segment VII has progressed to 5 cm. This heterogeneous response, with persistent multifocal disease and one progressing focus, makes a complete R0 resection of all initial metastatic sites unlikely while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage, though selective local strategies may be considered.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Reassessment of systemic strategy
• The progressing segment VII lesion indicates partial resistance to current chemotherapy.
• Adaptation of systemic therapy should be discussed in MDT to regain global disease control.

B. Detailed restaging and mapping
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with comparison to baseline imaging to localize all initial sites, including the “disappeared” lesions.
• Assess the precise anatomy of the progressing segment VII lesion and overall tumor distribution.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

C. Consideration of selective local treatment
• If systemic control is regained, a combined strategy may be considered:
– Parenchymal-sparing resection of the progressing segment VII lesion.
– Possible ablation/resection of other accessible stable lesions.
• The objective would be cytoreduction rather than complete clearance unless all initial sites can be addressed.

D. If global control cannot be achieved
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local ablative techniques for symptomatic or dominant lesions.
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as local ablative techniques or intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Case_Content:
Woman, 59 years old, metastatic rectal adenocarcinoma with initial bilobar involvement. After 6 cycles FOLFOXIRI: complete disappearance of lesions at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA normal.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response, need to assess risk of occult residual disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (oncologically)  
- Rationale:  
  • Technical criteria are fulfilled – current CT shows no detectable hepatic lesions and the future liver remnant (FLR) would be >30 % if any limited resection were required.  
  • Oncologic criteria are uncertain because a radiologic complete response after intensive chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI) does not guarantee eradication of microscopic disease; literature reports residual tumor in the majority of “disappearing” lesions.  
  • Therefore the case is not deemed outright resectable (R0 resection of known disease) but is amenable to curative‑intent surgery after confirmation of disease status, placing it in the “potentially resectable” category.

A. Confirmatory restaging  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast (gadoxetate‑enhanced) and a PET‑CT to verify the absence of residual hepatic and extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Review pre‑chemotherapy imaging to map the original locations of all liver metastases.  

B. Surgical exploration with intra‑operative ultrasound (IOUS)  
   - Schedule a laparotomy (or minimally invasive approach if expertise available) for liver exploration.  
   - Use IOUS to detect any occult lesions at the sites of the original metastases.  

C. Parenchyma‑sparing resection or targeted ablation  
   - If IOUS identifies residual disease, perform anatomic or non‑anatomic resection (segmentectomy/wedge) of the involved segment(s) ensuring:  
        • Negative macroscopic and microscopic margins (R0).  
        • Preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments, adequate inflow/outflow, and FLR ≥ 30 % (or FLR/body‑weight > 0.5 %).  
   - If lesions are sub‑centimetric or in difficult locations, consider intra‑operative radiofrequency/ microwave ablation as adjunct.  
   - If FLR would be insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) and a staged hepatectomy.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 additional cycles of FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) to treat potential micrometastatic disease, given the high risk of occult residual disease after a radiologic CR.  
   - Continue regular follow‑up: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach targeting the original metastatic locations, not only visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to detect occult residual disease.
• Depending on distribution, a staged approach may be required.

• Continue systemic therapy and close imaging surveillance.
• Consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal strategy.

-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• If surgery is performed, resume systemic therapy to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer with bulky metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy: incomplete reduction, persistence of three lesions >5 cm. CEA 450 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Partial response insufficient, no criteria for immediate resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Rationale:  
  • Three hepatic lesions remain >5 cm after 8 cycles of chemotherapy, indicating substantial tumor burden that likely precludes an immediate R0 resection while preserving two contiguous liver segments and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No explicit evidence of extra‑hepatic disease, but the MDT noted “bulky metastases” and lack of immediate resectability criteria, suggesting that technical factors (size, possible bilobar distribution) are currently limiting.  
  • The persistent high CEA (450 ng/mL) and only partial radiologic response imply aggressive biology, but also indicate that further systemic control may convert disease to a resectable state.  
  • According to current oncologic criteria, resectability hinges on achieving an R0 resection with adequate inflow/outflow and FLR; these conditions are not yet met, but may become attainable with additional conversion strategies (e.g., portal vein embolization, staged hepatectomy).  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Optimize systemic therapy  
   - Switch to a second‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFIRI ± anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR agents based on molecular profile) to attempt further tumor shrinkage and assess disease biology.  
   - Rationale: progression on first‑line therapy is a contraindication to immediate surgery; a different regimen may achieve better downsizing and provide a clearer prognostic signal.  

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, triphasic CT, and PET‑CT to delineate lesion size, exact segmental location, vascular involvement, and to detect occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Calculate FLR volume (CT volumetry) and assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT).  
   - Rationale: precise anatomical and functional data are essential to decide between single‑stage, two‑stage, or ALPPS approaches and to confirm absence of contraindicating extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Conversion/augmentation procedures (if imaging permits)  
   - If lesions are bilobar with insufficient FLR, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the tumor‑bearing lobe to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
   - If disease remains multifocal after PVE or FLR remains <30 %, evaluate a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future remnant plus PVE; second stage: resection of the diseased lobe).  
   - In selected patients with limited liver reserve and good performance status, ALPPS may be considered, recognizing its higher morbidity.  
   - Rationale: these techniques expand the pool of patients who can achieve an R0 resection while preserving adequate liver function.  

D. Surgical resection  
   - Once adequate tumor shrinkage and FLR are confirmed, proceed to curative‑intent liver resection aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
   - Plan primary colon resection either simultaneously (if primary tumor is symptomatic or low operative risk) or in a staged fashion (colon first if obstruction/bleeding risk, liver‑first if extensive hepatic disease).  
   - Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy should be resumed to address micrometastatic disease.  
   - Rationale: combined resection of primary and hepatic disease offers the only chance for long‑term survival in stage IV colorectal cancer.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had bulky liver metastases. After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, there is only partial reduction with persistence of three large lesions >5 cm and persistently elevated CEA (450 ng/mL). The residual tumor burden and limited response make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• The insufficient response to current chemotherapy requires modification of the systemic regimen or consider intra arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary cancer, according to MDT decision.
• The objective remains to achieve further tumor downsizing that may open a future surgical window.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Given the high CEA level (450 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, reducing lesion size and allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains insufficiently responsive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, operated two years earlier with a right hepatectomy for synchronous metastases from a left colon cancer. Surveillance: CEA 220 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two lesions segments II and III (2.1 and 3.4 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Contralateral liver recurrence, anatomically accessible, no extra-hepatic disease.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Two metachronous lesions (2.1 cm and 3.4 cm) are confined to segments II and III, anatomically accessible for a left‑lateral segmentectomy.  
  • Prior right hepatectomy leaves only the left liver; removal of segments II‑III would leave segment IV (and possibly caudate) as the future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Current oncologic criteria require preservation of at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and a FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy was given). Without volumetric data the FLR is uncertain and may be marginal, therefore the case is deemed potentially but not unequivocally resectable.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is identified, satisfying the oncologic component of resectability.  
  • KRAS mutation indicates a more aggressive biology, reinforcing the need for careful selection and systemic control before definitive surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative functional and volumetric assessment  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with liver volumetry to calculate the FLR after planned resection of segments II‑III.  
   - Perform liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin), indocyanine‑green clearance or LiMAx if available, and assess performance status/comorbidities.  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % after prior chemotherapy) and liver function is adequate, proceed to step B. If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization of the left portal branches (to hypertrophy segment IV) or a staged approach (e.g., ALPPS or two‑stage hepatectomy with ablation of one lesion).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy

C. Re‑evaluation after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat MRI (and PET‑CT if indicated) to assess tumor response and FLR volume.  
   - If disease is stable or responding and FLR remains adequate, proceed to surgery; if progression occurs, reconsider systemic‑only strategy or alternative locoregional therapies.  

D. Surgical plan  
   - Aim for an R0 resection:  
     • Anatomical segmentectomy of segment V (or non‑anatomic wedge if margin can be achieved).  
     • Local excision/wedge of the recurrence at the prior segment VII scar, preserving surrounding parenchyma.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to delineate lesion margins and vascular relationships.  
   - If calculated FLR after planned resection would be <30 % (or <20 % in a pristine liver), consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy; alternatively, treat one lesion with percutaneous ablation to spare liver tissue.  
   - Rationale: achieves complete macroscopic clearance while respecting the technical criteria of FLR, inflow/outflow, and biliary drainage.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy for 3–6 months as adjuvant therapy.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for surveillance.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define the relationship of the segment VII recurrence to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and scar tissue.

• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

• Given the elevated CEA (410 ng/mL) and recurrence, a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.

B. Combined local treatment strategy
• Given the scar location and technical difficulty, a combined approach is appropriate:
– Either Parenchymal-sparing resection or thermo-ablation of the segment V lesion.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Case_Content:
Woman, 55 years old, history of left hepatectomy for synchronous metastases. Surveillance: CEA 560 ng/mL. Liver MRI: multiple lesions in right and left lobes (up to 4.5 cm). RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Diffuse liver recurrence, potentially non-curative.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Bilobar disease with multiple lesions up to 4.5 cm in both right and left lobes indicates a high tumor burden.  
  • Prior left hepatectomy reduces the available hepatic parenchyma, raising concern for an insufficient future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • No volumetric data are provided; without confirmation that an FLR ≥ 30 % (or liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio > 0.5 %) can be preserved, a single‑stage curative resection is technically unsafe.  
  • Elevated CEA (560 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology, although RAS wild‑type is favorable.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but its presence would shift the case to unresectable.  
  • According to current oncologic criteria (adequate inflow/outflow, negative margins, sufficient FLR), the case does not meet definitive resectability but may become resectable after down‑staging and liver hypertrophy strategies.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   - Initiate intensive first‑line regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type and high CEA, aiming for tumor shrinkage and control of micrometastatic disease.  
   - Rationale: Down‑staging can reduce lesion size/number and improve the chance of achieving an R0 resection; systemic therapy also addresses occult disease.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment (4–6 weeks after 2–3 cycles)  
   - Repeat liver MRI with volumetry, CT chest/abdomen, and CEA measurement.  
   - Determine FLR percentage; assess response per RECIST.  
   - Rationale: Objective response and adequate FLR are prerequisites for any surgical plan.  

C. Liver hypertrophy strategy (if FLR < 30 % but potentially augmentable)  
   - If FLR is borderline, perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the diseased lobe or consider ALPPS/partial ALPPS in a high‑volume center.  
   - Rationale: Induces rapid hypertrophy of the future remnant, converting a borderline case to resectable.  

D. Surgical approach (contingent on response and FLR)  
   - If adequate down‑staging and FLR achieved, proceed with a staged hepatectomy (two‑stage or ALPPS) aiming for complete macroscopic clearance (R0/R1) while preserving ≥ 2 contiguous segments.  
   - If disease remains diffuse despite maximal down‑staging, abort curative surgery and continue systemic therapy (potentially with liver‑directed locoregional treatments such as radiofrequency ablation or Y‑90 radioembolization).  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPEOX) to eradicate residual microscopic disease.  
   - Ongoing CEA surveillance and imaging every 3–6 months.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver recurrences (up to 4.5 cm) after a prior left hepatectomy, without reported extrahepatic disease. The tumor burden, bilobar distribution in a previously reduced liver, and multiplicity of lesions make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory preoperative vascular and anatomical assessment
• Given the high CEA level (560 ng/mL) and multifocal recurrence, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy.
• The objective is disease control rather than immediate curative intent.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.

C. Consideration of selective local treatment only if major response occurs
• If significant tumor downsizing occurs, reassess feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections or ablative strategies for dominant lesions.
• Any surgical consideration would be secondary to systemic disease control.

D. If disease remains diffuse
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains diffuse, consider palliative or symptom-oriented local approaches as appropriate.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, right hepatectomy in 2021 for three KRAS mutated metastases. Liver MRI 2025: two new lesions segments IVb and II (2.7 and 3.2 cm).No other lesion at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 300 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar liver recurrence, sufficient liver volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Technical justification:  
  • Prior right hepatectomy has left a left liver remnant that includes segments II, III, IVa, IVb and caudate; the two new lesions are confined to segment II (3.2 cm) and segment IVb (2.7 cm).  
  • Both lesions are amenable to parenchyma‑sparing non‑anatomic or segmental resections while preserving at least two contiguous segments (e.g., segments III and IVa) with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
  • Imaging indicates sufficient future liver remnant (>30 % of total liver volume), satisfying the technical criteria for safe hepatectomy.  
- Oncologic justification:  
  • KRAS‑mutated disease, high CEA (300 ng/mL) and prior hepatic recurrence indicate aggressive tumor biology, which places the case in a high‑risk category.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease on thoraco‑abdominal CT, but the high tumor marker and bilobar recurrence argue for systemic disease control (“proof of time”) before definitive surgery.  
  • Therefore, while technically feasible, the case is best regarded as potentially resectable pending response to neoadjuvant therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (2–3 months)  
   • Regimen: FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab (or FOLFOX + bevacizumab if tolerability is a concern).  
   • Goal: achieve radiologic stability or response, treat occult micrometastases, and obtain a dynamic assessment of tumor biology (CEA trend, RECIST).  

B. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   • Repeat liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and chest CT (or PET‑CT) to confirm absence of new lesions and to re‑measure the two hepatic metastases.  
   • Re‑calculate future liver remnant; if FLR remains adequate, proceed; if FLR is marginal, consider portal vein embolization of the right portal branch (already resected) or left portal embolization of the segment to be preserved.  

C. Surgical resection (once disease control is documented)  
   • Perform a left‑lateral segmentectomy (or wedge resection) of segment II and a non‑anatomic resection of segment IVb with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance to achieve R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
   • Preserve segments III and IVa (and caudate) to maintain ≥2 contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
   • If the primary colorectal tumor has not yet been resected and is resectable, consider a simultaneous colorectal resection (e.g., low anterior resection) provided the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   • Resume the same systemic regimen (or a suitable alternative) for 3–6 months post‑operatively, tailored to tolerability and postoperative recovery.  
   • Continue KRAS‑directed management (no EGFR‑targeted agents).  
   • Serial CEA monitoring every 6–8 weeks and imaging at 3‑month intervals for the first year.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, history of segmental VI-VII resection. Liver MRI: new lesion segment III (2.4 cm) and micronodule segment II. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous contralateral recurrence, possible minimally invasive approach depending on remnant volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable  
- Justification:  
  • Technical criteria: disease is confined to segments II and III of the left liver; a parenchymal‑sparing resection of the 2.4 cm lesion in segment III with preservation of segments II and IV would leave at least two contiguous segments with inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
  • Oncologic criteria: metachronous recurrence, BRAF wild‑type, limited tumor burden (≤2 lesions), no reported extra‑hepatic disease – all favor a curative intent approach.  
  • Prior right posterior (VI‑VII) resection reduces overall liver volume; without volumetric data the future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed to exceed the generally accepted ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % of body weight) threshold, hence the case remains “potentially” rather than definitively resectable.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Obtain high‑resolution hepatobiliary MRI with volumetric analysis of the FLR.  
   - Perform liver function testing (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin) and assess performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
   - Complete systemic staging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET‑CT if indicated) to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Rationale: confirms that the FLR is sufficient and that no distant disease precludes curative surgery.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional)  
   - If FLR is borderline (<30 % or functional reserve limited) or if there is concern about aggressive biology, give 2–3 cycles of an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (e.g., CAPOX) ± anti‑EGFR or anti‑VEGF biologic, depending on KRAS status.  
   - Re‑image after chemotherapy to assess tumor response (“proof of time”).  
   - Rationale: may down‑size the segment III lesion, treat micrometastatic disease, and provide a safety net against early progression.  

C. Surgical phase  
   - Primary procedure: minimally invasive (laparoscopic or robotic) anatomical or non‑anatomical resection of the segment III metastasis with ≥1 mm negative margin.  
   - Adjunctive local therapy: percutaneous image‑guided thermal ablation (RFA/MWA) of the micronodule in segment II.  
   - If intra‑operative FLR assessment remains inadequate, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left lobe before definitive resection (two‑stage approach).  
   - Rationale: achieves R0 resection of the dominant lesion while preserving liver parenchyma; ablation treats the sub‑centimeter focus without further loss of volume.  

D. Post‑operative systemic therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX) once wound healing is adequate, unless contraindicated.  
   - Schedule surveillance imaging (MRI or CT) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, with CEA monitoring.  
   - Rationale: high recurrence risk after hepatic metastasectomy; adjuvant therapy improves disease‑free survival.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, operated two years earlier with a left hepatectomy.Liver MRI: recurrence segment VIII (3.1 cm) in contact with the middle hepatic vein. CEA 200 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Isolated complex recurrence of the hepatic dome, technical assessment required.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Technically, a solitary 3.1 cm lesion in segment VIII can be removed with a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy; the middle hepatic vein is involved but preservation or limited reconstruction is often feasible when adequate inflow/outflow to the remaining right‑lobe segments (V, VI, VII) can be maintained.  
  • After a prior left hepatectomy, the future liver remnant (FLR) consists of the right‑lobe parenchyma; removal of segment VIII would still leave at least two contiguous segments (V and VI/VII) with presumed sufficient volume, but quantitative volumetry is required to confirm that the FLR will be ≥20‑30 % of total liver volume (adjusted for any chemotherapy‑associated liver injury).  
  • Oncologically, the disease is solitary, no extra‑hepatic lesions are reported, and an R0 resection is achievable; however, the markedly elevated CEA (200 ng/mL) and prior recurrence suggest aggressive biology, warranting confirmation of disease stability before definitive surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Pre‑operative functional and volumetric assessment  
   - Obtain liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance (or LiMAx), and a contrast‑enhanced MRI/CT with 3‑D reconstruction to calculate FLR volume and delineate vascular anatomy, especially the relationship of the tumor to the middle hepatic vein.  
   - Rationale: ensures that the remaining liver will sustain postoperative function and defines whether portal vein embolization (PVE) or venous reconstruction is needed.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate 2–3 months of a standard peri‑operative regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) and monitor CEA trend.  
   - Rationale: high CEA indicates possible occult systemic disease; chemotherapy provides a test of tumor biology, may down‑size the lesion, and treats micrometastases.  

C. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat MRI/CT and CEA measurement. Confirm that the lesion remains solitary, unchanged or reduced in size, and that no new intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease has appeared.  
   - Rationale: progression would shift the plan toward non‑surgical systemic management; stability supports proceeding to resection.  

D. Surgical intervention  
   - Perform a parenchymal‑sparing segmentectomy of segment VIII with intent of R0 resection.  
   - If the middle hepatic vein is infiltrated, consider:  
     • Limited resection of the involved vein segment with primary repair or patch reconstruction, or  
     • Preservation of the vein by dissecting the tumor off the wall if negative margins can be achieved.  
   - In case FLR is borderline, combine the resection with intra‑operative portal vein embolization of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left‑over segments, or use adjunctive ablation for marginal disease.  
   - Rationale: achieves complete tumor clearance while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and adequate inflow/outflow, fulfilling technical resectability criteria.  

E. Post‑operative adjuvant therapy and surveillance  
   - Resume systemic chemotherapy (total 6 months peri‑operative) based on pathology and response.  
   - Schedule CEA and cross‑sectional imaging every 3–6 months for the first two years, then annually.  
   - Rationale: addresses residual microscopic disease and monitors for early recurrence, which is common after repeat hepatectomy.

Case_Content:
Man, 72 years old, right hepatectomy 4 years ago. Current liver MRI: multiple nodules segment III, 1-2 cm. CEA 550 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Multifocal recurrence, assessment of resectability and local alternatives.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable / borderline.  
- Justification:  
  • Disease is limited to multiple 1‑2 cm nodules confined to segment III of the left liver, satisfying the oncologic goal of complete (R0) extirpation.  
  • Prior right hepatectomy leaves only the left liver (segments II‑IV) as functional parenchyma; removal of segment III alone would preserve segments II and IV, meeting the technical requirement of at least two contiguous segments with inflow/outflow.  
  • However, the future liver remnant (FLR) after segment III resection may fall below the generally accepted 30 % of total liver volume for a non‑cirrhotic liver, especially in an elderly patient. Without volumetric data the FLR adequacy cannot be confirmed.  
  • High CEA (550 ng/mL) indicates aggressive biology; while RAS‑wild‑type permits anti‑EGFR therapy, the elevated marker raises concern for occult extra‑hepatic disease, which would downgrade resectability.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Obtain contrast‑enhanced MRI with hepatobiliary agent plus triphasic CT of chest/abdomen/pelvis; consider PET‑CT to exclude extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Perform liver volumetry (CT‑based) to calculate FLR after a hypothetical segment III resection.  
   - Evaluate liver function (bilirubin, AST/ALT, albumin, ICG clearance, platelet count) and patient performance status (ECOG).  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate a conversion regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + cetuximab) given RAS‑wild‑type status, aiming for tumor shrinkage and to test disease biology.  
   - Monitor CEA trend; a ≥50 % decline after 2–3 cycles suggests favorable biology.  

C. Re‑assessment after 2–3 months  
   - Repeat imaging and volumetry.  
   - If disease is stable or responding and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected), proceed to local therapy.  
   - If FLR remains insufficient, consider hypertrophy‑inducing strategies (e.g., left portal vein embolization – though limited by prior right hepatectomy – or ALPPS‑type staged approach if anatomy permits).  

D. Local definitive treatment  
   - Preferred: parenchymal‑sparing anatomical segment III resection (segmentectomy) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm negative margins.

   - Aim for R0 margins; intra‑operative frozen section if needed.  

E. Adjuvant and surveillance  
   - Continue systemic therapy post‑operatively for a total of 6 months (or longer per oncologic protocol).  
   - Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.
