• If disease remains controlled, perform ultrasound-guided left lateral sectoriectomy (rection of segments II and III) aiming for R0 margins.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: initially unresectable (potentially convertible)  
- Justification:  
  • Nine bilobar metastases exceed the simple technical threshold for a single‑stage R0 resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments.  
  • MRI demonstrates infiltration of the right portal pedicle, violating the essential criterion of preserving vascular inflow/outflow to the future liver remnant (FLR).  
  • Bilobar distribution and likely insufficient FLR (<20‑30 % of total liver volume) make an immediate curative hepatectomy unsafe.  
  • According to current criteria, resectability requires (a) R0 clearance of all disease, (b) preservation of two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow, and (c) adequate FLR; these conditions are not met at presentation.  
  • However, modern conversion strategies (systemic chemotherapy, portal vein embolization, two‑stage or ALPPS procedures) can convert a subset of such patients to resectable status, therefore the disease is deemed “potentially resectable after down‑staging.”

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   – Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because KRAS is mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
   – Goal: tumor shrinkage, assessment of disease biology, and potential clearance of microscopic disease.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (2–3 months after chemotherapy)  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with volumetry, triphasic CT of chest/abdomen, and PET‑CT to rule out additional extra‑hepatic sites.  
   – Calculate FLR; if FLR remains <30 % and right portal pedicle involvement persists, plan adjunctive hypertrophy techniques.  

C. Hypertrophy induction and staged hepatic resection  
   – If disease response is adequate and portal pedicle invasion is limited to a resectable segment, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the contralateral lobe to induce hypertrophy of the future remnant.  
   – Alternatively, for rapid hypertrophy, an ALPPS approach may be employed, provided the patient’s performance status and comorbidities allow.  
   – After sufficient FLR hypertrophy (target ≥30 % functional liver), proceed with a two‑stage hepatectomy or single‑stage extended resection aiming for R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to guide lesion clearance and possible adjunctive ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   – If the primary is asymptomatic and the patient tolerates major liver surgery, adopt a “liver‑first” strategy: complete hepatic clearance first, then perform an oncologic right hemicolectomy (T4N2) with adequate lymphadenectomy.  
   – If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or there is concern for rapid progression, consider simultaneous resection (if liver surgery is limited) or a “colon‑first” approach followed by hepatic surgery after recovery.  

E. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   – Following R0 hepatic and colorectal resections, resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) for a total of 6‑12 months, tailored to response and tolerability, to address micrometastatic disease.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with nine bilobar liver metastases associated with infiltration of the right portal pedicle and a very high CEA (2500 ng/mL) in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer. The combination of extensive bilobar disease and portal pedicle involvement precludes the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable at this stage.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2500 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is tumor downsizing and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response and reassess vascular relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) and evaluate venous outflow preservation or need for reconstruction.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only if a major response occurs with regression of portal pedicle involvement and significant reduction in tumor burden.
• Any surgical consideration would remain highly selective and dependent on restoration of clear vascular anatomy.

E. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and/or consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• If disease remains extensive, consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Woman, 61 years old, T3N1M1 rectal tumor, three liver metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII). CEA 680 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type. Liver MRI: extension to the hepatic vein confluence.
MDT Discussion: Metastases near venous confluence, high surgical risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Three metastases (segments IVa, VI, VIII) are technically resectable but are located at the hepatic‑vein confluence, a high‑risk vascular area requiring complex resection or reconstruction.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, satisfying the oncologic criterion of disease limited to the liver.  
  • Adequate future liver remnant (FLR) cannot be confirmed from the data; central lesions often leave <30 % FLR without pre‑operative augmentation, thus the case is borderline.  
  • KRAS‑mutated, high CEA (680 ng/mL) and synchronous presentation are adverse prognostic factors that favor a neoadjuvant “proof‑of‑time” approach before definitive surgery.  
  • The MDT notes “high surgical risk,” supporting the need for down‑staging or volumetric augmentation before a curative resection.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic induction chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   – Rationale: aims to reduce tumor burden, assess tumor biology, and potentially convert central lesions to a safer resection plane; anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated because of KRAS mutation.  

B. Restaging imaging (triphasic CT or liver‑specific MRI) after induction therapy, including volumetric analysis of the FLR and assessment of vascular involvement.  
   – Rationale: determines response, confirms whether a margin‑negative (R0) resection is feasible, and quantifies the need for liver‑volume augmentation.  

C. Pre‑operative liver‑volume augmentation if FLR < 30 % (e.g., portal vein embolization or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy – ALPPS).  
   – Rationale: improves postoperative liver function and reduces risk of hepatic insufficiency in a patient already deemed high‑risk.  

D. Definitive hepatic resection (likely extended right hepatectomy or central hepatectomy with hepatic‑vein reconstruction) performed first (liver‑first strategy) once adequate FLR is secured and disease is controlled.  
   – Rationale: the liver surgery is the more technically demanding component; addressing it before rectal surgery avoids delay caused by potential postoperative complications of a major hepatectomy.  

E. Rectal cancer management – after hepatic recovery (≈4–6 weeks):  
   1. Neoadjuvant long‑course chemoradiotherapy (if not already given) to down‑stage the T3N1 rectal lesion.  
   2. Restaging of the pelvis; proceed to curative‑intent rectal resection (low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision) or, if sphincter involvement mandates, abdominoperineal resection.  
   – Rationale: standard of care for locally advanced rectal cancer; sequencing after liver surgery prevents interruption of systemic therapy and allows full recovery from the major hepatic operation.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., continuation of oxaliplatin‑based regimen ± bevacizumab) for 3–6 months post‑both surgeries, tailored to response and tolerability.  
   – Rationale: addresses micrometastatic disease and improves disease‑free survival, especially important given KRAS mutation and high pre‑operative CEA.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with four bilobar liver metastases. CEA 900 ng/mL, RAS wild-type. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion invading the IVC over 1 cm.
MDT Discussion: Caval invasion requiring multidisciplinary surgical evaluation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
   Technical factors – four bilobar metastases can be addressed if an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved (≥30% of total liver volume or >0.5 FLR/body‑weight ratio).  
   Vascular factor – one lesion in segment VII invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over 1 cm; IVC involvement is not an absolute contraindication but requires complex vascular reconstruction and increases peri‑operative risk, thus moving the case from “up‑front resectable” to “potentially resectable” pending down‑staging and detailed vascular planning.  
   Oncologic factors – high CEA (900 ng/mL) suggests aggressive biology; however, RAS wild‑type and left‑sided primary allow use of anti‑EGFR therapy, supporting a neoadjuvant approach to assess disease biology.  
   No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but its presence would shift classification to unresectable; therefore, current data are insufficient to declare outright resectability.  

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) for 8–12 weeks, given RAS wild‑type left‑sided tumor.  
   - Rationale: maximize tumor shrinkage, potentially reduce IVC invasion, and serve as a “test‑of‑time” to gauge tumor biology.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, CT‑angiography of the IVC, and volumetric CT to calculate FLR.  
   - Include chest CT/PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Rationale: determine response, re‑evaluate IVC involvement, and confirm that an FLR ≥30% (or >350 g) can be achieved.  

C. Pre‑operative liver hypertrophy strategy (if FLR insufficient)  
   - Perform portal vein embolization (PVE) of the liver segments planned for resection, or consider ALPPS if rapid hypertrophy is needed and patient fitness permits.  
   - Rationale: increase FLR to meet safety thresholds before major hepatectomy.  

D. Surgical phase – liver‑first approach  
   - If post‑chemotherapy imaging shows adequate downsizing and FLR is sufficient, proceed with curative‑intent liver resection:  
      En bloc resection of segment VII lesion with IVC segment resection and reconstruction (using PTFE or autologous graft) while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with intact inflow/outflow.  
      Combine with non‑anatomic or anatomical resections of the remaining three metastases to achieve R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
   - Rationale: address the most technically demanding component first; ensures that any postoperative hepatic insufficiency does not compromise subsequent colorectal surgery.  

E. Colorectal primary management  
   - After hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), perform definitive resection of the left‑sided colon cancer (segmental colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy).  
   - If intra‑operative assessment shows the primary is asymptomatic and liver surgery was limited, a simultaneous resection could be considered, but staged approach is preferred given the complexity of the liver operation.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Resume/continue chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) with anti‑EGFR for an additional 3–6 months, tailored to postoperative recovery and pathology.  
   - Rationale: eradicate microscopic disease and address the high pre‑operative CEA level, which correlates with recurrence risk.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four bilobar liver metastases, including a segment VII lesion invading the IVC over ~1 cm, without reported extrahepatic disease. While the number of lesions is limited, true caval invasion makes a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection unlikely without complex vascular resection/reconstruction and carries high operative risk. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable only in a highly selected setting, after tumor downsizing and multidisciplinary vascular assessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of all lesions with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (900 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate FOLFOXIRI combined with anti-EGFR therapy given RAS wild-type status as discussed in MDT.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Marked reduction in lesion size and number.
– Separation from the IVC.
– Feasibility of R0 resection with or without partial IVC resection with acceptable future liver remnant, potentially requiring staged hepatectomy with or without portal vein embolization.
• Multidisciplinary evaluation with vascular surgery is required to assess feasibility of partial IVC resection/reconstruction if needed.

C. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• One or two-stage hepatectomy or extensive parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• If regression of caval invasion occurs or reconstruction is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of all lesions.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or graft reconstruction.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Surgical management of the primary tumor
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, five liver metastases including one 8.5 cm in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 870 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis with bilateral portal contact, complex technical discussion.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Five hepatic metastases, including an 8.5 cm central lesion in segment IVb with bilateral portal vein contact – technically challenging but not an absolute contraindication under current criteria.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, fulfilling the oncologic requirement that all known disease can be cleared.  
  • Resectability hinges on ability to preserve ≥2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow, biliary drainage and a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % (or FLR/body‑weight ratio > 0.5). The size and central location raise concern for insufficient FLR and vascular margins, thus requiring volumetric assessment and possibly hypertrophy strategies.  
  • High CEA (870 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest aggressive biology; neoadjuvant chemotherapy is needed to test disease control before committing to surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate intensive chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) given KRAS mutation (anti‑EGFR agents ineffective).  
   - Goal: tumor down‑staging, assess tumor biology, and potentially reduce the 8.5 cm lesion.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment (4–6 weeks after 2–3 cycles)  
   - Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and CT chest/abdomen/pelvis to confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic lesions.  
   - Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or <0.5 g/kg), plan hypertrophy.  

C. Hypertrophy strategy (if needed)  
   - If FLR insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) of the lobe bearing the majority of disease, or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) with clearance of the future remnant liver in the first stage.  
   - ALPPS may be an option in highly selected patients with rapid hypertrophy need, but only after multidisciplinary consensus given its higher morbidity.  

D. Surgical resection  
   - Aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions while preserving at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow.  
   - Preferred approach: anatomic right or extended right hepatectomy combined with segment IVb/IVa resection, contingent on FLR adequacy; otherwise, staged or parenchymal‑sparing resections with intra‑operative ultrasound guidance.  
   - Simultaneous resection of the primary colon tumor can be considered if the patient’s performance status permits and the colon lesion is resectable without increasing operative risk; otherwise, adopt a “liver‑first” sequence to avoid progression of hepatic disease.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (e.g., continuation of the pre‑operative regimen) for 3–6 months as adjuvant therapy.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging every 3–4 months for the first two years.

• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the segment IVb lesion to both portal branches.

• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis

Case_Content:
Man, 73 years old, transverse colon tumor, two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 70 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Normal CEA despite high volume, question regarding biological sensitivity for follow-up.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Two liver metastases measuring 4.2 cm and 4.8 cm are within the size limits that can be removed with curative intent, provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume) can be preserved.  
  • RAS‑wild‑type and BRAF‑wild‑type status are favorable biologic predictors for response to conversion chemotherapy and for long‑term survival after resection.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but imaging confirmation is required.  
  • Age 73 y alone does not preclude surgery, yet performance status, comorbidities, and hepatic functional reserve are not provided; these factors could shift the case to unresectable if poor.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and a PET‑CT to (i) delineate exact segmental location of each metastasis, (ii) calculate FLR, and (iii) exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
   - Perform a full clinical assessment: ECOG performance status, Charlson comorbidity index, baseline liver function tests, and cardiopulmonary evaluation.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (conversion/intention‑to‑cure)  
   - Initiate a doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) given the RAS/BRAF wild‑type profile.  
   - Duration: 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles) to assess tumor biology (“proof of time”) and to potentially downsize lesions, improving the chance of an R0 resection and allowing a margin‑sparing approach.  

C. Restaging after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Repeat MRI/PET‑CT to evaluate response (RECIST) and re‑calculate FLR.  
   - If disease remains confined to the liver, lesions are still resectable, and FLR is adequate, proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  

D. Surgical sequencing  
   - Option 1 – Simultaneous resection: If the primary transverse colon tumor is resectable with low operative risk and the liver resection can be performed with ≤ 2‑stage hepatectomy, consider a combined colon and liver operation.  
   - Option 2 – Staged approach: Prefer a “liver‑first” strategy when the liver disease is the dominant threat to survival or when the colon surgery may delay hepatic resection. Perform liver resection first (segmental or lobar resection achieving R0 margins), followed by colon resection 4–6 weeks later after recovery.  
   - Choose the approach based on intra‑operative assessment of FLR, patient’s physiological reserve, and multidisciplinary consensus.  

E. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen or a fluoropyrimidine‑based regimen) for 3–6 months, tailored to pathological response and margin status.  
   - Enroll in surveillance protocol: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (4.2 and 4.8 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. Both lesions are limited in number and appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± cetuximab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if major hepatectomy is considered.

D. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of the primary tumor
• Either combined or staged transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, left T4N1M1 colon cancer, six liver metastases (up to 5.6 cm) at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 1400 ng/mL. KRAS G12C mutation confirmed.
MDT Discussion: Specific molecular profile, may benefit from a later targeted strategy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
The patient is classified as potentially resectable (borderline‑resectable). Rationale:  
- Six hepatic metastases (≥5 cm total burden) exceed the classic “≤4 lesions” rule, but modern criteria allow resection if an R0 margin can be achieved and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 20‑30 % of total liver volume or ≥0.5 % of body weight) can be preserved.  
- No imaging data are provided on the lobar distribution, proximity to major vessels/ biliary structures, or calculated FLR, so technical feasibility cannot be confirmed.  
- The primary tumor is T4N1, indicating locally advanced disease that will also require oncologic resection; this adds to the surgical burden.  
- High CEA (1400 ng/mL) and KRAS G12C mutation suggest aggressive biology, favoring a neoadjuvant (down‑staging) approach before definitive surgery.  
- No explicit extra‑hepatic metastases are described; if present, they would shift the case toward unresectable unless limited and amenable to curative treatment.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (conversion chemotherapy) – Start a KRAS‑mutant‑appropriate regimen (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2‑3 months, aiming for tumor shrinkage and biological response assessment. Anti‑EGFR agents are contraindicated because of KRAS mutation.  

B. Restaging and functional liver assessment – After 2‑3 months repeat high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI with liver‑specific contrast, and calculate FLR (volumetry). Evaluate response (RECIST) and check for new extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Decision point  
   • If sufficient tumor regression and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight) with clear vascular and biliary margins → proceed to curative‑intent surgery.  
   • If FLR is inadequate but disease is otherwise resectable → plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, followed by re‑assessment.  
   • If disease remains extensive or progresses → continue systemic therapy, consider locoregional options (Y‑90 radioembolisation, hepatic arterial infusion, or percutaneous ablation) and reassess for possible later conversion.  

D. Surgical sequence –  
   1. Primary tumor resection (left‑sided colon) – either simultaneous with liver resection if patient fitness permits, or staged (colon first) to control the T4 primary and allow recovery before major hepatectomy.  
   2. Liver resection – aim for R0 removal of all metastases using an anatomic or parenchymal‑sparing approach; preserve at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage. If lesions are bilobar, a two‑stage hepatectomy (resect one lobe, allow hypertrophy, then resect the second) may be required.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy (including the induction cycles). Consider enrollment in a clinical trial of KRAS‑G12C targeted agents (e.g., sotorasib) or add postoperative bevacizumab if not used pre‑operatively, based on multidisciplinary consensus.

Case_Content:
Man, 57 years old, low T3N2M1 rectal cancer, four peripheral liver metastases (2-3.5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 90 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS, positive circulating tumor cells.
MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating cells despite low volume, prognostic significance discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline resectable)  
• Technical justification: four peripheral liver metastases, each ≤ 3.5 cm, amenable to anatomic or non‑anatomic resections; likely to preserve ≥ 30 % future liver remnant (FLR) provided adequate volumetry. No major vascular or biliary involvement described.  
• Oncologic justification: synchronous presentation, T3 N2 primary, elevated CEA (90 ng/mL) and presence of circulating tumor cells indicate aggressive biology; however RAS‑wild type and MSS are favorable. These high‑risk features argue for neoadjuvant systemic therapy (“proof of time”) before committing to curative surgery.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy – 2–3 months of a doublet (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given RAS‑wild type. Goal: tumor‑size reduction, assessment of chemosensitivity, and eradication of micrometastases.  
B. Neoadjuvant radiotherapy for the rectal primary – short‑course (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiation depending on sphincter involvement and distance from mesorectal fascia; performed either concurrently with chemotherapy (if using short‑course) or sequentially after induction chemotherapy.  
C. Restaging (6–8 weeks after systemic therapy) – high‑resolution liver MRI with liver volumetry, repeat pelvic MRI, and chest CT to confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic disease and to calculate FLR.  
 • If all lesions remain resectable with adequate FLR → proceed to curative surgery.  
 • If FLR would be < 30 % → consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) before definitive resection.  
D. Surgical phase – preferred reverse (liver‑first) approach because the liver disease dictates the oncologic timeline and the rectal tumor is low‑lying but can be controlled with radiotherapy.  
 1. Hepatic resection – perform parenchymal‑sparing resections (segmental or non‑anatomic) to remove all four metastases with R0 margins, preserving ≥ 2 contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
 2. Rectal surgery – 6–8 weeks after liver operation (or after recovery from PVE/TSH if performed), perform low anterior resection with a protective diverting loop ileostomy; if sphincter involvement is confirmed, consider abdominoperineal resection.  
E. Adjuvant therapy – postoperative continuation of systemic chemotherapy (total 6 months) and consider maintenance anti‑EGFR therapy based on postoperative pathology and response.

Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (2–3.5 cm) without reported extrahepatic disease. The lesions are limited in number and anatomically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is resectable. The presence of circulating tumor cells suggests higher systemic risk but does not alter technical resectability.

A. Preoperative staging and integration with rectal management
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define vascular and biliary relationships and calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment (chemoradiotherapy).

B. Mandatory peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the presence of circulating tumor cells indicating systemic dissemination risk, administer 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is treatment of micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 2-3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Surgical management after restaging : management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N2 rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

E. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider either parenchymal-sparing wedge/segmentectomy or ablation if no biliary or large vessels proximity) aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvis MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.

Case_Content:
Woman, 68 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥10 lesions) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2700 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Massive liver disease with high marker elevation, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Current classification: Potentially resectable (borderline/unresectable at presentation but convertible)  
- Rationale:  
  • ≥10 hepatic lesions, most likely bilobar, would require resection of >70 % of liver parenchyma to achieve R0, violating the technical criteria of preserving at least two contiguous segments and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in normal liver).  
  • No volumetric data are provided; without confirmation that an FLR of ≥30 % can be preserved, an upfront hepatectomy is not feasible.  
  • High CEA (2700 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive tumor biology, supporting the need for systemic down‑staging before any surgical attempt.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but the absence of a thorough extra‑hepatic work‑up (lung, peritoneum) precludes a definitive “resectable” label.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Systemic conversion chemotherapy  
   – Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) for 2–3 months to assess tumor biology and attempt downsizing of hepatic disease.  
   – Rationale: improves resectability rates, provides a “test‑of‑time” for disease aggressiveness, and may reveal occult extra‑hepatic sites.  

B. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform contrast‑enhanced MRI of the liver (or liver‑specific MRI) plus chest CT/PET‑CT to evaluate response, lesion size, distribution, and to rule out extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   – Obtain volumetric CT to calculate FLR.  
   – Rationale: determines whether sufficient hepatic reserve exists and whether a curative‑intent resection is technically possible.  

C. If adequate down‑staging and FLR ≥30 %  
   – Portal vein embolization (PVE) or Associating Liver Partition and Portal vein Ligation for Staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy of the future liver remnant, followed by a two‑stage hepatectomy (or single‑stage extended resection if FLR becomes adequate).  
   – Rationale: allows safe removal of extensive bilobar disease while preserving liver function.  

D. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   – If the primary lesion is symptomatic or at risk of obstruction/bleeding, consider simultaneous colon resection during the second hepatic stage (or a staged colon resection after hepatic clearance).  
   – Rationale: eliminates the source of further metastatic seeding and aligns with oncologic principles for synchronous disease.  

E. Post‑operative/adjuvant therapy  
   – Continue systemic chemotherapy (potentially with targeted agents) for 3–6 months after hepatic and colonic surgery, tailored to response and tolerability.  
   – Rationale: eradicates microscopic residual disease and addresses systemic risk.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with ≥10 liver metastases in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and very high CEA (2700 ng/mL). The tumor burden, multiplicity of lesions, and likely bilobar distribution preclude the possibility of achieving a complete R0 resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and vascular assessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to define precise vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (2700 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI after 3-6 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in the rare situation of major radiologic and biologic response with significant reduction in number and size of lesions allowing parenchymal-sparing resections.

D. If disease remains extensive
• Continue second-line systemic therapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented management according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T3N1M1 colon cancer at the abdominal CT scan, three liver metastases (2-3 cm) and confirmed left portal invasion on liver MRI. CEA 310 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Unilateral portal involvement, potentially approachable depending on volume.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Three hepatic metastases (2‑3 cm) are limited in number and size, which meets technical criteria for resection.  
  • All lesions are unilateral and appear confined to the left hepatic lobe; preservation of the right lobe would satisfy the requirement of at least two contiguous segments and an adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 %).  
  • Confirmed left portal vein invasion introduces a vascular involvement that may necessitate portal vein resection/ligation or pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the right lobe; this makes the case borderline rather than outright resectable.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, but a full staging work‑up (chest imaging, PET/CT) is still required to confirm liver‑only disease.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy – Administer 2–3 months of intensive doublet or triplet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology, achieve possible downsizing of hepatic lesions, and treat occult micrometastatic disease.  
B. Restaging and functional assessment – Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with volumetry and CT of chest/abdomen; calculate FLR volume. If FLR remains <30 % after anticipated resection, proceed to portal vein embolization of the right portal branch to induce hypertrophy of the left lobe (or vice‑versa depending on final surgical plan).  
C. Surgical sequencing –  
   • If the primary left‑sided colon tumor is symptomatic or high‑risk, perform a staged approach: first a curative colon resection (laparoscopic or open), followed by liver surgery after systemic therapy and FLR optimization.  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic and the patient is fit, a simultaneous resection (colon + right hepatectomy) can be considered, provided operative time and physiologic stress are acceptable.  
   • Liver surgery: aim for right hepatectomy (removing left‑lobe disease) with en‑bloc portal vein resection/reconstruction if tumor involves the left portal branch, ensuring negative (R0) margins.  
D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy – Resume postoperative systemic chemotherapy (potentially with targeted agents based on molecular profile) for 3–6 months, and monitor CEA and imaging every 3–6 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, right T3N0M1 colon tumor, single 5.6 cm metastasis in segment VIII, in close contact with IVC at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 540 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Large central metastasis, major technical question regarding surgical approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Single lesion, solitary, therefore no limitation by number.  
  • Size 5.6 cm exceeds the historic 5 cm cut‑off but current criteria prioritize R0 resection and adequate future liver remnant (FLR) rather than absolute size limits.  
  • Lesion is in segment VIII, a right‑lobe segment; a non‑anatomic or segmental resection would preserve > 50 % of liver volume, satisfying the technical requirement of ≥ 30 % FLR (or liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio > 0.5).  
  • Proximity to the inferior vena cava (IVC) raises concern for vascular involvement; if the tumor merely abuts the IVC without true invasion, a parenchymal‑sparing resection with vascular control is feasible. If invasion is present, vascular reconstruction would be required, moving the case toward “potentially resectable” pending response to systemic therapy.  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease; therefore, oncologic criteria are not violated.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  

A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (3–4 months)  
   - Regimen: FOLFOXIRI ± cetuximab (RAS wild‑type) or FOLFOX + cetuximab.  
   - Goals: (i) assess tumor biology (CEA trend, radiologic response), (ii) attempt downsizing of the lesion away from the IVC, (iii) treat micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging work‑up after chemotherapy  
   - Multiphasic liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and intra‑operative ultrasound planning.  
   - High‑resolution CT angiography to delineate IVC involvement.  
   - Volumetric analysis of FLR; calculate liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio.  
   - Full extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT/PET) to confirm absence of distant disease.  

C. Surgical sequencing  
   - If the primary right‑colon tumor is asymptomatic (no obstruction or bleeding), adopt a liver‑first approach:  
        • Segment VIII anatomical/segmental resection aiming for R0 margins.  
        • If the tumor contacts but does not invade the IVC, use vascular control (Pringle, IVC clamping) and perform a wedge resection with negative margins; reconstruct IVC only if full‑thickness invasion is confirmed intra‑operatively.  
        • Employ intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm clearance and to detect occult lesions.  
   - After hepatic recovery (≈ 4–6 weeks), perform definitive right‑hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy).  

D. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (6 months) tailored to pathology (margin status, response).  
   - Consider continuation of anti‑EGFR therapy if the tumor remained RAS wild‑type and responded.  

E. Contingency plan  
   - If restaging shows progression, invasion of IVC, or insufficient FLR, shift to non‑surgical local control (e.g., percutaneous ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy) combined with systemic therapy, rather than proceeding to high‑risk hepatectomy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 5.6 cm liver metastasis in segment VIII in close contact with the IVC, without reported extrahepatic disease. Although solitary, the central location and caval proximity make a standard parenchymal-sparing R0 resection technically demanding and potentially unsafe without prior tumor downsizing or vascular planning. From a hepatobiliary oncologic perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable, but only after careful vascular assessment and likely induction therapy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI to define exact segmental distribution of the lesion with detailed vascular and biliary relationships. 
• Given the high CEA level (540 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Intensive conversion systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Initiate 2–3 months of induction chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is significant tumor downsizing, reduction in number/volume of lesions, and clearance from the IVC to enable potential surgical planning.

C. Close radiologic monitoring
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2-3 months to assess response, particularly:
– Relationship of lesions to the IVC.
– Global reduction of liver tumor burden.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Monitor CEA kinetics as an indicator of treatment response.

D. Surgical management if feasibility is confirmed
• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesion to the IVC and hepatic veins.
• If regression occurs or vascular control is deemed feasible, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection of segment VIII, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible IVC tangential resection or reconstruction with multidisciplinary discussion with vascular surgery to assess feasibility of tangential IVC resection if needed.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

E. Management of primary tumor
• After recovery, perform right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon cancer) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. If insufficient response
• Continue systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Case_Content:
Woman, 65 years old, T4N1M1 rectal tumor, four liver metastases at the abdominal CT scan, CEA 60 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Immuno-sensitive profile, discussion on optimal therapeutic sequence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: potentially resectable (borderline).  
- Rationale:  
  • Four hepatic lesions are present; number alone does not preclude resection if adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, satisfying the oncologic criterion for curative intent.  
  • Technical feasibility cannot be confirmed without data on lesion size, segmental distribution, proximity to major vessels/ducts, and volumetric assessment of the FLR.  
  • Given the need for a major hepatectomy (likely >2 segments) to clear four metastases, pre‑operative strategies such as portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy may be required, placing the case in the “potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast, chest CT, and liver volumetry to define lesion anatomy, FLR percentage, and to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
   – Assess baseline hepatic function (bilirubin, INR, albumin) and patient performance status (ECOG, comorbidities).  

B. Systemic therapy with immunotherapy‑based regimen  
   – Initiate pembrolizumab (or nivolumab) as first‑line for MSI‑H metastatic CRC, combined with FOLFOX (or FOLFOX‑bevacizumab) if rapid tumor shrinkage is desired.  
   – Goal: achieve disease control, obtain “proof of time,” and possibly down‑size liver metastases to facilitate R0 resection.

   – Deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiation depending on sphincter involvement and patient tolerance.  
   – This addresses the T4 lesion, reduces local recurrence risk, and allows the liver‑first approach without delaying definitive rectal surgery.

   – If FLR ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 % body weight) and all lesions are amenable to R0 resection, proceed with hepatic surgery:  
        • Preferred: liver‑first (reverse) strategy – perform hepatectomy first (single‑stage if FLR sufficient, otherwise PVE or two‑stage approach).  
        • If major hepatectomy required and FLR insufficient, schedule PVE followed by delayed resection.  
   – After hepatic clearance, complete rectal surgery (low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, or abdominoperineal resection if sphincter involvement) within 6–12 weeks.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   – Continue immunotherapy (or switch to maintenance pembrolizumab) post‑operatively for at least 12 months, per MSI‑H guidelines.  
   – Consider postoperative FOLFOX for 3–6 months if high‑risk features persist (e.g., positive nodes, T4).

• Consider parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided liver resections only if residual lesions persist and complete clearance is feasible with adequate future liver remnant.

• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic immunotherapy (including the pre operative cycles).

Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1300 ng/mL, KRAS mutated. Liver MRI: contact with right hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Superior vascular invasion, significant operative risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Technical criteria – eight bilobar lesions, contact with the right hepatic vein and superior vascular invasion make an R0 resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments and adequate inflow/outflow unlikely with a single‑stage hepatectomy.  
  • Functional criteria – no volumetric data are provided, but with multiple bilateral lesions the future liver remnant (FLR) would probably be <30 % of total liver volume, which is below the safety threshold for major resection.  
  • Oncologic criteria – T4 primary, N2 nodal disease, KRAS mutation, very high CEA (1300 ng/mL) indicate aggressive biology; these factors favor a neoadjuvant approach to test disease control before committing to extensive liver surgery.  
  • Therefore, the disease is not outright unresectable (conversion strategies exist) but cannot be resected safely at present without down‑staging and/or hypertrophy techniques.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start intensive conversion chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) for 2–3 months.  
   - Rationale: aims to shrink tumor burden, assess tumor biology (“test of time”), and potentially convert lesions away from major vessels; KRAS‑mutated disease still responds to oxaliplatin/irinotecan‑based regimens.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and triphasic CT; include volumetric analysis of FLR.  
   - Perform PET‑CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum).  
   - Evaluate liver function (bilirubin, ICG clearance, ALBI score) and patient performance status (ASA, cardiopulmonary reserve).  
   - Rationale: determines whether sufficient down‑staging and FLR have been achieved to proceed to surgery or whether further conversion is needed.  

C. Hypertrophy‑inducing procedure and staged hepatic resection (if imaging shows residual bilobar disease but FLR remains inadequate)

   - Combine resection with local ablative modalities (RFA or microwave) for lesions abutting the right hepatic vein that are not amenable to safe transection.  
   - Rationale: creates a safe FLR (>30 % in chemotherapy‑treated liver) while allowing complete clearance of all visible disease with negative margins.

   - If the primary is asymptomatic and the liver‑first approach is adopted, proceed with hepatic clearance first, then perform a curative‑intent right hemicolectomy after hepatic recovery (typically 4–6 weeks).

   - After complete (R0) hepatic and colorectal resections, resume systemic therapy (e.g., maintenance capecitabine ± bevacizumab) for at least 6 months, tailored to molecular profile and postoperative recovery.

Woman, 55 years old, left colon cancer, multiple bilobar metastases at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 2100 ng/mL, BRAF wild-type, HER2 amplified.
MDT Discussion: Particular molecular profile, possible sensitivity to an anti-HER2 approach.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline)  
- Justification:  
  • Bilobar distribution and multiple lesions are technically challenging but not an absolute contraindication when an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver) can be preserved.  
  • The patient is relatively young (55 y) and has a left‑sided primary, both factors associated with higher conversion and resection rates.  
  • BRAF wild‑type status is favorable for achieving resectability.  
  • No data are provided on FLR volume, lesion size, number, vascular involvement, liver function, performance status, or extra‑hepatic disease; therefore a definitive “resectable” label cannot be assigned without further work‑up.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive baseline assessment  
   - Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast to define number, size, and relationship of all metastases.  
   - Calculate FLR using volumetric CT or MRI; consider portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR is <30 % (or <40 % after extensive chemotherapy).  
   - Perform full staging (CT chest, PET‑CT if indicated) to exclude or characterize extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Record ECOG/ASA, comorbidities, liver biochemistry, and baseline CEA.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy tailored to molecular profile  
   - Initiate HER2‑directed regimen (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab or trastuzumab + lapatinib/tucatinib) combined with a doublet chemotherapy backbone (FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   - Rationale: HER2 amplification predicts sensitivity to anti‑HER2 therapy; combining with chemotherapy maximizes tumor shrinkage and provides “biologic proof‑of‑time.”  
   - Plan for 3–4 months (≈6–8 cycles) of therapy, monitoring CEA trend and radiologic response.  

C. Re‑assessment of resectability after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Repeat MRI/CT to evaluate tumor burden reduction, FLR adequacy, and any new lesions.  
   - If sufficient down‑staging achieved and FLR acceptable, proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery; if not, consider additional cycles, alternative systemic options, or locoregional therapies (Y‑90 radioembolization, hepatic arterial infusion).  

D. Surgical phase  
   - Option 1 – Single‑stage hepatectomy (if disease becomes amenable to R0 resection with adequate FLR).  
   - Option 2 – Two‑stage or ALPPS (if lesions are dispersed and FLR needs augmentation). Include intra‑operative ultrasound, use of parenchymal‑sparing techniques, and consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  
   - Perform simultaneous or staged resection of the primary left‑sided colon cancer based on symptomatology and oncologic timing (e.g., “liver‑first” approach if primary is asymptomatic).  

E. Post‑operative management  
   - Continue HER2‑targeted therapy in the adjuvant setting (e.g., trastuzumab ± pertuzumab) for at least 6 months, combined with standard adjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX) as tolerated.  
   - Serial CEA and imaging surveillance every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, T3N1M1 upper rectal tumor, liver metastases (3-5 cm) with contact with IVC and right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 580 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Complex central metastases, discussion on combined approach or venous reconstruction.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Justification:  
  • Oncologic factors – synchronous T3N1 rectal cancer, high CEA (580 ng/mL), and central liver lesions abutting the IVC and right hepatic vein indicate high‑risk disease but do not constitute absolute contraindications.  
  • Technical factors – contact with major vascular structures makes a standard anatomic resection unsafe without vascular control; however, modern hepatic surgery permits IVC/RHV resection and reconstruction when a negative margin can be obtained and adequate inflow/outflow preserved.  
  • Future liver remnant (FLR) is not reported; if ≥30 % of functional liver can be preserved after a right‑sided or extended right hepatectomy, the case remains technically feasible.  
  • No extra‑hepatic disease is described; absence of distant metastases would satisfy the oncologic criterion for resection.  

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab).  
   - Rationale: assess tumor biology, achieve possible down‑staging of vascular involvement, and treat micrometastatic disease.  

B. Restaging and volumetric assessment (contrast‑enhanced liver MRI, CT chest/abdomen, and liver volumetry).  
   - Rationale: determine response of the hepatic lesions, quantify FLR, and confirm absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease.  

C. Pre‑operative liver optimization (if FLR <30–35 %):  
   - Portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy of the left liver.  
   - Rationale: ensure sufficient postoperative liver function for a major right‑sided resection.  

D. Definitive hepatic resection (liver‑first approach).  
   - Perform right or extended right hepatectomy with en‑bloc resection of the involved segment of IVC and right hepatic vein, followed by vascular reconstruction (prosthetic graft or autologous patch) as needed.  
   - Rationale: early control of the dominant metastatic burden; vascular reconstruction is feasible in experienced centers and preserves oncologic clearance.  

E. Rectal cancer management (after hepatic recovery, typically 4–6 weeks).  
   - Long‑course chemoradiotherapy (if not already given) followed by low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision.  
   - Rationale: allows completion of systemic therapy, avoids delay of liver surgery, and addresses the primary tumor once the patient has recovered from the major hepatectomy.  

F. Adjuvant systemic therapy (post‑operative FOLFOX or similar) for at least 6 months.  
   - Rationale: consolidate response, treat residual microscopic disease, and improve disease‑free survival.

  • Oncologic criteria are met – three liver metastases, no documented extra‑hepatic disease, RAS wild‑type, MSS, and primary located in the left colon (favorable for curative intent).  
  • Technical criteria are compromised – MRI shows invasion of the hepatic vein confluence, indicating loss of outflow for at least one hepatic sector. Preservation of adequate venous drainage is essential for R0 resection.  
  • The ability to preserve two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and to achieve an FLR ≥ 30 % cannot be confirmed without volumetric data.  
  • Therefore, the case is not outright resectable but may become resectable after down‑staging, vascular reconstruction, or staged hypertrophy strategies.

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
   - Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + anti‑EGFR antibody) given RAS wild‑type status.  
   - Goals: tumor shrinkage, assessment of disease biology (“proof of time”), and potential conversion of vascular involvement to a resectable pattern.  

B. Restaging and functional assessment  
   - Perform contrast‑enhanced CT and liver‑specific MRI with volumetry to calculate future liver remnant (FLR) and delineate the exact extent of hepatic vein invasion.  
   - Evaluate liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, AST/ALT, platelet count) and patient performance status (ECOG/ASA).  

C. Pre‑operative liver augmentation if needed  
   - If FLR is <30 % after anticipated resection, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  

D. Surgical resection  
   - Once adequate FLR and disease control are confirmed, proceed to curative‑intent hepatectomy with en‑bloc resection of involved hepatic vein(s) and reconstruction (e.g., interpositional graft or patch).  
   - Decide between simultaneous colon and liver resection versus staged approach based on intra‑operative risk and patient fitness; a staged approach is preferred if major vascular reconstruction is required.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance systemic therapy  
   - Resume postoperative chemotherapy (same regimen or adapted) for 3–6 months to eradicate microscopic disease.  

F. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA measurements and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first two years, then at increasing intervals.

• Repeat high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of lesions to the hepatic vein confluence.

• If significant regression occurs, plan an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing resection with the aim of R0 margin.
• Anticipate possible venous reconstruction or complex vascular control.

Woman, 56 years old, right T3N1M1 colon cancer, four liver metastases (3-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 780 ng/mL, non-V600E BRAF mutation (D594G).
MDT Discussion: Atypical BRAF mutation, intermediate prognosis, bilobar liver involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable.  
- Technical justification: Four metastases (3‑5 cm) are bilobar but number and size alone do not preclude resection if a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % can be preserved; parenchymal‑sparing resections or staged hepatectomy are feasible.  
- Oncologic/biologic justification:  
  • Synchronous disease, right‑sided primary, N1 nodal status, very high CEA (780 ng/mL) and a non‑V600E BRAF D594G mutation are adverse prognostic factors that favor initial systemic therapy to test tumor biology (“proof of time”).  
  • No documented extra‑hepatic disease, but this must be confirmed.  
- Therefore, while a curative‑intent liver resection is technically possible, the case is best regarded as borderline/potentially resectable pending response to neoadjuvant therapy and confirmation of adequate FLR.

Step 2 – Recommended strategy  
A. Comprehensive restaging  
   - Perform liver‑specific MRI with hepatobiliary contrast, chest‑CT or PET‑CT, and baseline laboratory panel (including liver function, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation).  
   - Calculate FLR volume (CT volumetry) and assess portal venous anatomy.  

B. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (4–6 cycles)  
   - Preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (triplet chemotherapy with anti‑VEGF) given the aggressive biology; consider adding a BRAF‑targeted agent (e.g., encorafenib + cetuximab) if a clinical trial is available, recognizing that D594G is atypical and may respond to EGFR inhibition.  
   - Goal: tumor down‑staging, assess treatment response, and allow observation of disease kinetics.  

C. Re‑assessment after neoadjuvant therapy  
   - Repeat MRI/CT to evaluate size reduction, number of viable lesions, and FLR.  
   - If FLR is insufficient, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) as needed.  

D. Surgical phase  
   - Primary tumor: Right hemicolectomy (open or laparoscopic) performed either simultaneously with liver resection if patient fitness permits, or as a staged procedure (primary first, then liver).  
   - Liver: Parenchymal‑sparing, anatomic or non‑anatomic resections to achieve R0 margins; consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or combined liver‑first approach if FLR is borderline.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance; apply intra‑operative ablation (RFA/MWA) for lesions that are technically unresectable but amenable to local control.  

E. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume systemic therapy post‑operatively for 3–6 months (same backbone, possibly de‑escalated).  
   - Enroll in a BRAF‑directed clinical trial if available; consider immunotherapy only if mismatch repair deficiency is identified.  

F. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

MDT Discussion: Presence of circulating tumor cells despite no visible extension, prognostic value discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability Assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable (borderline‑resectable)  
- Rationale:  
  • Six hepatic metastases (2–4 cm) do not exceed technical limits; modern techniques allow resection of multiple, bilobar lesions provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR ≥ 30 % or FLR/body‑weight > 0.5).  
  • No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease, satisfying the oncologic criterion of complete macroscopic clearance.  
  • High‑risk biological features (T4 primary, N2 nodes, CEA 320 ng/mL, circulating tumor cells positive) suggest aggressive disease, favoring a neoadjuvant “proof‑of‑time” approach before definitive surgery.  
  • Without volumetric data or clear segmental distribution, a single‑stage resection cannot be confirmed; therefore the case remains potentially resectable pending further assessment and possible liver‑hypertrophy strategies (PVE, two‑stage hepatectomy, ALPPS).

Step 2 - Recommended strategy  
A. Induction systemic therapy (8–12 weeks)  
   - Regimen: FOLFOXIRI + cetuximab (RAS‑wild type) or FOLFOX + cetuximab if tolerability is a concern.

B. Restaging and functional assessment (after induction)  
   - High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast plus triphasic CT.  
   - Volumetric calculation of FLR; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS).

C. Surgical plan (based on restaging)  
   - If all lesions become resectable with adequate FLR: proceed to single‑stage anatomic/segmental hepatectomy aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm acceptable) while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments.

   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to detect occult lesions; consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  

D. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - Resume or continue systemic therapy for an additional 3–6 months post‑resection, tailored to response and tolerability.  
   - Serial CEA and circulating tumor cell monitoring every 3 months; imaging surveillance (CT/MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years.
